articles.title_orig: What share of plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
articles.title_zh: What share of plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
articles.content_orig:
Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:
Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.
The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.
The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.
From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.
People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
But it tells us none of that.
It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index.
When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable.
As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most.
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
When people think about global oil, their minds often go toward countries in the Middle East.
But it’s the United States that is the world’s largest oil producer.
The chart shows oil production by country since 1990. As you can see, the US has been the largest producer for the last nine years, since it overtook Saudi Arabia.
Production in the US gradually declined during the 1990s and early 2000s, then increased sharply after 2010 and is now at an all-time high.
This data comes from the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy .
In 2025, the amount of foreign aid given by the world’s richest countries fell by almost a quarter . That amounted to a reduction of roughly US$50 billion.
Aid cuts in the United States — and the shutdown of its agency for international development, USAID — got the most attention, and for good reason: the US is the world’s largest aid donor in dollar terms, so its contributions make a huge difference to the global total.
But many other countries cut their aid contributions, too. In the chart, you can see the change among the largest 10 donors (in dollar terms) from 2024 to 2025. This is given as a share of their gross national income.
Contributions fell in eight of the ten countries. Only Sweden and Italy increased their budgets.
The countries shown are the largest donors in dollar terms; some others not shown contribute far more in relative terms: Norway, for example, was the only country to give more than 1% of its national income to foreign aid.

articles.title_orig: Trump hits International Criminal Court with sanctions after Nobel goes to former judge
articles.title_zh: Trump hits International Criminal Court with sanctions after Nobel goes to former judge
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday revisited his argument that he deserves to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this year, telling reporters in the Oval Office that he has done “far more” than any other U.S. President.
“I don't know what their decision is going to be. They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” Trump said , insisting that it would be a “great discredit” to the Norwegian Nobel Committee if they do not announce him as the recipient Friday morning.
“I've stopped maybe the total obliteration of the world, because Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, and that's a positive thing,” he claimed, listing the reasons why he believes he is deserving of the prestigious prize.
Trump said he was “very honored ​to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more” than him. The 2025 winner , Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado , notably gave her medal to Trump in January as she pressed the U.S. to support democracy in Venezuela, days after the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores .
Following the regifting of the medal, the Norwegian Nobel Committee emphasized that “the prize itself—the honor and recognition—remains inseparably linked to the person or organization designated as the laureate by the Norwegian Nobel Committee.”
Trump has long said he is deserving of the prize. The leaders of Israel , Cambodia , and Pakistan have all previously said they nominated Trump. However, all nominations remain private and the Norwegian Nobel Institute doesn’t release a shortlist of contenders. Still, each year, names are circulated in public discourse and bets are made as to who might come out on top.
The Norwegian Nobel Institute has registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s prize, of which 208 are individuals and 79 are organizations.
As Trump’s war with Iran stretches into its eighth month, polls have tipped him as an unlikely contender to walk away with this year’s award. Amid mounting speculation over who may be the chosen recipient, here’s a look at some of the contenders.
The start of Sudan’s current civil war in April 2023 escalated an already desperate humanitarian crisis . Fighting between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in late 2025 pushed civilians further toward risk of famine , with even more people displaced and killed .
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms have provided desperately needed relief. The collapse of the state and increasingly difficult access for humanitarian groups over the past three years has led to a rise of 700 ERRs across all of Sudan’s 18 states, mobilizing over 26,000 volunteers, according to Alsanosi Adam , a journalist and ERR volunteer himself.
The community-led initiative provides healthcare, food assistance, education, civilian protection, and psychosocial support. According to Right Livelihood , volunteers have been detained and tortured while offering assistance.
The charity is a lead contender to win the Nobel Peace Prize, with Polymarket citing a 17% chance.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Office last April amid an emerging trade rift with Trump and threats from Washington to annex Canada and make it the 51st state .
The tariff threats escalated and, following the collapse of negotiations in August, the U.S. and Canada are now engaged in a trade war .
Carney has opened up new trading and diplomatic relations with China and Europe in an effort to move away from U.S. reliance. He delivered a defiant speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, denouncing “American hegemony” and insisting there has been a “rupture in the world order.”
Carney’s efforts to unite Canada in the face of Trump’s threats have seemingly helped his popularity at home, with his approval rating back up to 66%, according to new data from Liaison Strategies .
When it comes to the Nobel Peace Prize, he’s more an outsider, with a 1% chance of receiving the honor.
Pope Leo XIV , the first American pope , has made strident global outreach efforts since his ascension to the head of the Catholic Church in April 2025.
His repeated calls for peace, including his spotlight on Gaza , have made an impact, and even earned him criticism from Trump.
“Today, sadly, war has returned, even to Europe: a new senseless slaughter, claiming countless civilian lives every day,” Leo told European leaders in September, referencing the Russia-Ukraine war. “We must ask whether we are truly making creative efforts to advance world peace, or whether we are simply seeking to stem the tide of war and better prepare ourselves for wars that we assume are still to come.”
In the aftermath of the first U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, Leo said “stability and peace are not achieved through mutual threats, nor through the use of weapons, which sow destruction, suffering, and death, but only through reasonable, sincere, and responsible dialogue.”
Trump responded by falsely claiming that Leo would “be fine with Iran having a nuclear weapon”—Leo rejected the claim and urged critics to speak “truthfully.”
Pope Leo stands with a 1% chance of being awarded the prize.
Mykola Kuleba co-founded Save Ukraine in 2014 during the early days of the conflict in Eastern Ukraine. The organization’s work has become increasingly important since Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022.
Missing Ukrainian children have become a focal point of humanitarian efforts amid the war, with Moscow contending that it relocated children in an effort to protect them. Save Ukraine has so far helped reunite 1,763 children with their parents, but the organization has said thousands more need to be brought home.
“[Kuleba’s] work combines direct humanitarian action with strong advocacy for children’s rights, making him a compelling candidate for international recognition,” said Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), as he detailed his list of suggested candidates for the 2026 prize.
Kuleba is currently listed as having a 9% chance.
Yulia Navalnaya, widow of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, has become an activist in her own right, challenging President Vladimir Putin’s regime and fighting for democracy.
Alexei died in an Arctic penal colony in February 2024. A few weeks later, Yulia vowed to take up his cause in an interview with TIME , where she expressed hope that Russia might one day be a “normal, democratic country”—the future Alexei “dreamed about.”
Navalnaya is listed as having a 5% chance of winning the Nobel Peace Prize.

articles.content_orig:
The United States has imposed a new set of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), prompting several countries – including US allies – to condemn the move and reiterate their support for the world’s war crimes tribunal.
On Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington would be banning transactions with the “rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate”, adding that President Donald Trump would “never allow” the Hague to prosecute Americans.
The ICC was created in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when national authorities are unable or unwilling to do so.
The US Treasury Department announced the penalties with a six-month initial grace period and other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecommunications, software, pension payments and transactions related to detainees.
Rubio said the sanctions would give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns and would be adjusted if they did not meet those demands.
The Trump administration says the court has exceeded its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not ICC members, such as Israel. The United States and Israel have never joined the court.
In response to the sanctions, the ICC said that the move was an “assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order”. It called on its 125 member states to defend the institution.
“The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it,” the ICC said in a statement. “This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment.”
The Trump administration sanctioned more than a dozen judges and prosecutors before issuing sanctions on the court itself Friday.
Soon after the US announcement, top United Nations officials condemned the move.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres was “deeply alarmed” by the expected impact of the sanctions on the court as a whole, particularly its ability to carry out its mandate, a statement from his spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said.
“Today’s decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar,” the statement added.
UN Human Rights chief Volker Turk called for immediate measures to protect the ICC. “These sanctions – the latest in a series of retaliatory steps against the ICC and its personnel for the work they do every day to advance accountability for the very worst violations of human rights – are unacceptable,” he said.
ICC member states that are US allies also expressed dismay at the decision.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, whose country hosts the ICC, said the US’s decision was “deeply regrettable”.
“We will stand firm in defence of the court. At the same time, it’s important to note that the sanctions will not take effect immediately and that service providers can continue to work for the ICC. The six-month period before the sanctions take effect creates scope for dialogue,” he said.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Britain, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Japan said they “regret and strongly disagree” with the sanctions.
“If put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families … We remain both united in our support for the ICC and committed to engaging in constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-States Parties,” they said.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot also said Brussels would discuss support for the ICC with European Union foreign affairs colleagues on Monday and at the upcoming European Council.
“We will press for concrete protection. The court’s independence cannot depend on whom it investigates. Europe must act. Belgium is calling for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the court,” Prevot said.
Similarly, organisations and rights groups sounded the alarm over the implications of the US decision.
Philippe Bolopion, executive director of US-based Human Rights Watch, said the Trump administration had made clear its aim to “destroy” the ICC and “shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court”.
“The ICC was created to ensure that no one, no matter how powerful, is above the law. Governments that value human rights and accountability should condemn this outrageous move and take swift action to protect the ICC, its staff, and all those who cooperate with it, starting with the European Union using its laws to mitigate the sanctions’ impact in the region,” he said.
The Executive Director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, James Goldston, said the sanctions were a “calculated attack on the rule of law and the principles of judicial independence and equality that underpin it.”
“This is the latest move in a campaign of coercion intended to destroy the system of international justice,” he said.
Amnesty International called on countries to “resist”. Trump’s “sanctions are designed to isolate and ultimately destroy the International Criminal Court”, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty’s senior director for research, policy, advocacy and campaigns, said in a statement. “This existential attack must fail. States must take concrete action to resist the imposition of these measures.”
Amid widespread criticism, Israel commended the US move.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailed the sanctions and praised Trump and Rubio for taking this “critical decision”.
“The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty,” Netanyahu wrote on X.
In 2024 the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on war crimes and crimes against humanity charges for the war on Gaza.

articles.title_orig: Arkansas World War II soldier returns home after 84 years
articles.title_zh: Arkansas World War II soldier returns home after 84 years
articles.content_orig:
Updated: 05:07 EDT, 9 October 2026
A family who ditched the UK to spend eight years sailing around the world have revealed that their outgoings have doubled since they returned home.
In 2017, Alan Wood, 57, and his wife Irenka, 55, set sail on their 53-foot 1997 Amel Super Maramu sailboat from Greece when their children were just five, eight and 11.
Over the course of eight years, the family sailed more than 40,000 nautical miles through more than 40 countries and territories.
Now, the family have returned from their global adventure and are facing the reality of Britain's crippling cost of living - after becoming accustomed to spending just £1,500 in monthly outgoings at sea.
Since being home, that number has increased to nearly £3,000, due to increased energy bills, amenities and school expenses for their sons.
The two youngest children, brothers Darroch, 17, and Yewan, 14, are also now acclimating to full-time education and full access to phones and social media.
Alan, an author based in Brighton, East Sussex, said: 'It was an amazing adventure for us as a family, but the adjustment back to real life has taken us aback.
'Especially for our youngest, Yewan, who has spent more years of his life on sea than on land. When you go from bribing your way through the Suez Canal with fuel or fleeing from Sudanese pirates to a regular school day, it takes a moment!'
A family who ditched the UK to spend eight-years sailing around the world have revealed that their outgoings have doubled since they returned home
In 2017, Alan Wood, 57, and his wife Irenka, 55, set sail on their 53-foot 1997 Amel Super Maramu sailboat from Greece when their children were just five, eight and 11
Alan and Irenka decided to set off to Greece in 2017 after becoming 'tired of the rat race' in the UK.
'We had been seriously thinking about doing a long term sailing trip ever since Yewan was born. We reached a point where each of the kids were going to be entering a new stage of education and felt if we didn't do it then, we never would,' Alan said.
The couple put their Brighton home on the rental market, with the rent they received helping to cover the mortgage and some living expenses.
Alan explained: 'The rent on our place back in Brighton really helped see us through at first. But we'd also started making videos, just for ourselves, so when I'd go see a boat we might want to buy, I'd post the video online for Irenka to see it as well.
'Over time we decided to make more videos and it became a decent source of income over the eight years.'
During their travels, the family explored all corners of the world and embraced a slower pace of life.
The children were homeschooled for around two hours a day on the boat, though Alan added that 'their education was as much off the boat' as it was on it.
'Seeing wild seals in the Galapagos Islands was like a geography and biology lesson in one,' he said.
'Learning how to sail is all physics and they were constantly surrounded by new languages, cultures and foods.'
During their travels, the family explored all corners of the world and embraced a slower pace of life. The children were homeschooled for around two hours a day on the boat
Now, the family have returned from their global adventure and are facing the reality of Britain's crippling cost of living - after becoming accustomed to spending just £1,500 in monthly outings at sea
In May last year, the family decided to return to the UK. Their two youngest had reached ages where they needed to take exams, like A-levels and GCSEs, while the eldest, Rowan, had already been back in England studying since 2022
In May last year, the family decided to return to the UK. Their  two youngest had reached ages where they needed to take exams, like A-levels and GCSEs, while the eldest, Rowan, had already been back in England studying since 2022.
Alan said: 'Rowan had headed back to the UK about five years into the journey when she was 16 to complete her studies.
'The boys were now reaching an age where we'd want them to return back to a more normal life, get their qualifications, and grow up.
'We felt we'd given everything we could to this experience, and it gave back to us in equal measure.'
Now, back in Brighton for just over a year, the family are settling back into routine, with the boys in six-hour school days as opposed to two-hour sessions and access to more screens than ever before.
'To be honest it's been a bit of an assault on the senses, in a good and bad way!' Alan said.
'It's been an adjustment for the boys to get involved in school, not only academically as it's a whole new framework, but also socially in some ways.
'But the kids are very adaptable and have gotten used to things- especially being on phones and tablets!
'We were always out and about while sailing, but back home there's a lot of life that happens on screens, as we're learning.'
Irenka and Alan have also taken some time adjusting to life back in Britain. The cost of their weekly shop had doubled, and their energy bills soared, especially in direct comparison with using solar panels and a hydro generator on the boat.
Alan added: 'The effect of inflation hit us big time, especially as we're having trouble selling our boat because the market's pretty flat right now.
'Our weekly shops almost doubled in cost and the price of heat and electricity was truly stunning.
'Our old gas boiler was struggling so we turned to our wood burning stove and found that a dumpy bag of kiln dried logs was now well over £100.
'Additionally, water (which we had produced with a watermaker or rain catchers) and electricity (which we'd produced with solar panels and a hydro generator) were expenses we hadn't properly accounted for.'

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias now a major hurricane as it closes in. These cities will be hit hard.
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias now a major hurricane as it closes in. These cities will be hit hard.
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring heavy rain, damaging winds and life-threatening storm surge to the northern Gulf Coast when it makes landfall late Friday or early Saturday.
According to the National Hurricane Center, Isaias remains a Category 3 storm with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph, which forecasters consider a "major hurricane."
As of 5 p.m. ET, the storm was located about 90 miles south of Pensacola, Fla., and roughly 125 miles south-southeast of Mobile, Ala., moving north at 17 mph. It is expected to approach the northern Gulf Coast this afternoon and make landfall near the Alabama-Florida state line tonight.
The governors of Florida, Alabama and Georgia have declared states of emergency, along with several Mississippi counties, urging residents to take the first hurricane of an unusually quiet season seriously. Thousands of National Guard soldiers are being deployed.
Is the storm headed your way? Follow it in real time on the new Yahoo Weather app.
Mandatory evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Florida's Walton, Escambia, Okaloosa and Franklin counties. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey also ordered nonresidents to evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island.
Heavy rain and flooding could extend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina through the weekend. There's also a risk of tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle into southern Georgia.
Follow live updates on Hurricane Isaias below.
Areas experiencing increased tornado risks on Friday caused by Hurricane Isaias
The National Weather Service warned Friday that strong winds from Hurricane Isaias are increasing the risk of tornadoes in areas impacted by the storm.
"The greatest risk will be east of the center, particularly across the Florida Panhandle into southern Georgia," the NWS wrote in a public advisory Friday afternoon.
Forecasters expect tornado risk to continue into Saturday as the storm makes its way inland, spreading to new areas across Georgia and into the Carolinas.
According to the most recent advisory from the National Hurricane Center, as of 5 p.m. ET on Friday:
Hurricane Isaias was about 90 miles south of Pensacola, Fla., and roughly 125 miles south-southeast of Mobile, Ala.
The storm had maximum sustained winds of 115 mph
It was moving north-northeast at 17 mph
Isaias is expected to make landfall in the western Florida Panhandle later tonight.
"Little change in strength is expected before Isaias makes landfall this evening," the NHC said. "Weakening is expected to begin tonight after landfall, and Isaias is forecast to become post-tropical on Saturday."
President Trump is shown on the jumbotron before a college football game between Texas and Tennessee at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville on Sept. 26.
President Trump announced Friday that he will not be attending Alabama's pivotal college football matchup against Georgia in Tuscaloosa, Ala., on Saturday because of Hurricane Isaias.
"It is important to have our wonderful First Responders, Law Enforcement, and others, focused on that Storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the President of the United States, ME!" Trump wrote on Truth Social .
Earlier in the week, Trump had told reporters that he still intended to travel to the game, despite the impending storm.
"I love Alabama. I got to go to a game like that," he told reporters on Wednesday, but added that he would consider changing his plans "if there's an emergency."
There had been some speculation that the game might be postponed or relocated because of Isaias, but organizers have said it will be played as scheduled.
According to the most recent forecasts, Isaias will likely be downgraded to a tropical storm by the time it reaches Tuscaloosa on Saturday. The heart of the storm is expected to have moved north of the city by the time the game is scheduled to kick off at 7:30 p.m. ET.
Instead of traveling to Alabama, Trump said he will hold a rally in Tennessee on Saturday in support of Republican candidates for House, Senate and governor in the state.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced on Friday that the state had opened a hotline where residents can report "unconscionable increases in prices" by retailers in the hurricane's path.
"Protecting Floridians isn't a seasonal job," Uthmeier said in a press release . "Whether it's a storm, a scam, or a greedy corporation, our office will enforce the law."
Florida law prohibits price hikes on "essential commodities and services" that may be needed to prepare for or recover from a major storm, including food, water, ice, gasoline, lumber, equipment and hotel rooms.
Violators can be fined $1,000 for a first offense, with penalties increasing to $25,000 and potential criminal sanctions for severe offenders. Floridians can report suspected price gouging through MyFloridaLegal.com or by calling 1-866-9-NO-SCAM.
With Hurricane Isaias expected to make landfall on the northern Gulf Coast near the Alabama-Florida line, coastal Mississippians may be thinking they caught a break. But the state's governor doesn't want residents to let their guard down.
"We are still expected to receive some effects from the hurricane including 3-5' of storm surge in and around Biloxi through Jackson County and a strong risk of flash flooding throughout the eastern part of our state," Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves wrote in a post on X. "Continue to stay vigilant and weather aware, Mississippi!"
According to t he most recent advisory from the National Hurricane Center, as of 2 p.m. ET:
Hurricane Isaias was about 145 miles south of Pensacola, Fla., and roughly 125 miles southeast of the mouth of the Mississippi River
It had maximum sustained winds of 120 mph
It was moving north-northeast at 16 mph
Isaias is expected to approach the northern Gulf Coast this afternoon and make landfall somewhere near the Alabama-Florida line tonight.
"Fluctuations in intensity are possible through this afternoon, but Isaias is expected to be at or near major hurricane strength when it makes landfall this evening," the hurricane center said. "Weakening is expected beginning tonight after Isaias makes landfall, and the storm is likely to become post-tropical by late Saturday."
Want to know how to pronounce Isaias? Don't ask Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.
While delivering an update on preparations for Hurricane Isaiah, DeSantis said didn't know how to correctly pronounce the storm's name — and wasn't about to try.
"I don't know how to pronounce this because it's not normal," DeSantis said. "So, you know, I'm calling it Isaiah. You guys can call it what you want. I know that's not how you pronounce this. It's something else. But it's weird and I'm just going to keep butchering it for the next 72 hours."
For the record: Isaias, the Spanish form of Isaiah, is pronounced "ee-sah-EE-ahs."
In a livestream update from the National Hurricane Center in Miami, NHC Director Michael Brennan said tropical storm-force winds from Hurricane Isaias will begin reaching the Florida Panhandle within the next few hours.
"So if you are in these evacuation zones and you've been asked to leave by your local officials, please get out as soon as you can before conditions deteriorate," Brennan said.
A storm surge of up to 9 feet is likely, and rainfall totals of up to 15 inches are possible in the western Florida Panhandle, southwestern Georgia and southern Alabama.
He also urged those in the storm's path to use extra caution after it passes.
"Be careful with chainsaws," Brennan said. "Don't push yourself if you're out there in dangerous conditions. Please take care of yourself. And make sure if you're operating a generator, do it well away from your home and vent it away from your home to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning. So please stay safe."
Hurricane Isaias was the first to form in this year's Atlantic season, which begins in June and runs through November. It was one day shy of tying a 121-year-old record for the basin's latest-forming hurricane, accord

articles.title_orig: JD Vance says he won't watch livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
articles.title_zh: JD Vance says he won't watch livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
articles.content_orig:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s confirmation Thursday that the firing squad death of the Fort Hood mass shooter will be livestreamed was swiftly met with bipartisan outrage and questions over how the public execution will be carried out.
Firing squad executions are rare in the US (though they have been sparingly used as an alternative to lethal injection recently,) and public displays of the death penalty are even less common. The last public execution is considered to be the 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea , a Black man from Kentucky who was found guilty of raping a White woman by an all-White jury.
About 90 years later, on December 3 at 1 p.m. local time, the public will be able to watch Nidal Hasan’s death at Texas’ Fort Hood, where he killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting .
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec in an interview aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday.
But Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the execution would actually be livestreamed, saying, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.” He added that he would not watch the execution if it were livestreamed.
Vice President JD Vance on Friday said he won’t be watching the firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter if it’s live-streamed, and cast doubt on it being streamed.
Speaking to reporters Friday evening, President Donald Trump said the administration would make a determination about the livestream.
FCC chair Brendan Carr told CNBC’s “Squawk on the Street” it was his understanding that the execution would not be shown on broadcast TV – but that he would defer to Hegesth and “his decisions on how to move forward.”
Sheri Lynn Johnson, the assistant director of the Death Penalty Project at Cornell Law School, told CNN that while access to executions has been given to members of the media, the defendant’s counsel and, in some cases, their family members, allowing the public to watch could desensitize the public to death.
“It’s … particularly celebrating death in a very violent way, which seems to me both an additional infringement on the dignity of the person executed, and, and also something that hardens the public to the idea that murder is wrong or death is wrong,” Johnson said.
Here’s what we know so far about the scheduled livestream of Hasan’s execution.
Hasan’s death will be carried out by US “soldiers with rifles,” Hegseth said.
CNN asked the Pentagon several logistical questions, including who the soldiers would be, how they will be chosen and who will be running the livestream. The department said it will provide more details as it gets them.
Military death penalties and their methods must be approved by the president. Earlier this week, Trump agreed to Hegseth’s recommendation of a firing squad for Hasan. The move set up what would be the US Army’s first such execution of a soldier since World War II and the first imposition of any death penalty on an armed service member in 65 years.
More broadly, there have only been six firing squad executions since 1977, according to the Death Penalty Information Center . Three of them took place last year in South Carolina — 15 years after the previous one.
Firing squad executions could be making a comeback as a handful of US death penalty states explore alternatives to lethal injection, by far the nation’s dominant execution method.
States have faced several issues with lethal injection deaths, like legal challenges by inmates, inadequate supplies and failed executions, as seen recently in the case of Christa Pike , who survived an execution attempt in Tennessee. In comparison, experts say the firing squad is generally thought to be fast and effective. But the fact that the method is overtly violent has likely contributed to states’ hesitancy to use it.
Only five states permit a firing squad to be used for executions, according to the DPIC . As of July 2026, it is the main method in Idaho.
Timothy McVeigh, the man convicted of the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, had requested that his execution be televised nationally.
An entertainment company even filed a legal challenge to be able to live stream it, but a federal court rejected the attempt.
Ultimately, the execution by lethal injection was televised to a limited group of people that included survivors of the bombing and victims’ families.
Then-US Attorney General John Ashcroft , in his approval of the closed-circuit telecast, recognized that there are “precedential procedures” in televising the execution but made the case that the McVeigh case had “unique circumstances.”
According to reports from Amnesty International, which opposes the death penalty, public executions took place in Afghanistan and Iran in recent years. In 2025 , there were six public executions in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.
The organization has also said earlier this year that through interviews, it has learned that North Korea also uses the method “to terrorize entire communities into compliance.”
The announcement of Hasan’s public execution drew criticism from both sides of the aisle, with people making the case that America should not be like authoritarian countries where public executions more commonly take place.
Outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said in a post on X , “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”
Georgia GOP Rep. Austin Scott raised similar concerns, saying that while he supports the death penalty, “live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.”
Republican Sen. John Curtis on X highlighted the “bloody spectacles” that took place in ancient Rome, writing, “A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”
“Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite. The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity,” Curtis wrote. “Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent. I urge him to reconsider.”
Similarly, Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut called the plan “disgusting” and “medieval.”
“What is he mimicking ISIS executions?,” he told CNN’s Erin Burnett, referring to Hegseth.
The president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops called it a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death.”
“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” Archbishop Paul Coakley said in a statement .
Meanwhile, Joe Kent, a former high-ranking US intelligence official who resigned over the Iran war earlier this year, argued that Hasan’s death could be used as propaganda by terrorists.
“Streaming his execution is not just a stain on our morality—it also gives the terrorists free propaganda that they will use to radicalize & recruit more terrorists like” Hasan, Kent said in a post on X .
Peter Bergen, a CNN national security analyst, said the livestream could give terrorist groups material to “exploit.”
“If a video exists, groups will try to turn it into propaganda,” he said. Bergen, who has covered Hasan extensively, added that the gunman sees himself as a “religious warrior” and a “public video of his execution would play into his narrative of who he is.”
This story has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Haley Britzky, Dakin Andone and Alejandra Jaramillo contributed to this report.

Tennessee farmer and rancher Mitchell Kolinsky discusses the impact of high diesel prices on agricultural operations and his reaction to President Donald Trump's plans to lower energy costs.
President Donald Trump announced Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to "immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter."
Trump said the agreement came after the two had a "highly successful discussion."
He added on Truth Social, "Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel . Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
TRUCKING INDUSTRY HIT BY STRING OF BANKRUPTCY FILINGS AS DIESEL COSTS SURGE
Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to, according to President Donald Trump, "immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immedi (Kremlin Press Office/Anadolu via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Diesel prices have soared because of the wars in Iran and Ukraine , and Trump has been urged by Republicans to bring costs down before the midterms in November.
On Friday, Trump said at the White House: "The prices will come tumbling, and it’s all going to be over soon one way or the other," referring to the war in Iran .
AMERICANS HEATING THEIR HOMES THIS WINTER FACE A STARK COST DIVIDE
President Donald Trump signs an executive order temporarily expanding access to red-dyed diesel for highway use. (Win McNamee/Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
"They have no military. They have no navy, they have no air force, they have no anti-aircraft," he said. "We took out yesterday 28 million barrels. I think we took out more than we’ve ever taken out at any other time, including before the war. The Hormuz Strait . The Navy, we put a blockade up, nobody gets through."
OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES
A diesel fuel pump sits in a cradle at a gas station in Princeton, Ill. (Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File / Getty Images)
Last month, several trucking and freight businesses filed for bankruptcy as diesel reached an average of $6.26 per gallon across the country.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Conditions deteriorate on Gulf Coast
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias live updates: Conditions deteriorate on Gulf Coast
articles.content_orig:
States of emergency have been issued in parts of Alabama, Florida and Georgia, and up to 9 feet of storm surge is possible.
⛈️🌊 Track the storm, check your local risk and get more detailed timing from meteorologists in the CNN Weather app
• Conditions are deteriorating quickly along the Gulf Coast with Hurricane Isaias, a ferocious Category 3 storm, only hours from making landfall. Thousands of residents are without power and the storm surge is already being felt.
• Mandatory evacuations have been ordered in counties in Florida and Alabama, and several cities – including Mobile – are implementing curfews. More than 1.7 million people are under a tornado watch . President Donald Trump has canceled plans to attend the Alabama-Georgia football game Saturday in Tuscaloosa.
• Isaias is expected to cause widespread power outages and disrupt travel, with some airports , bridges and rail services closing during the storm. Nearly three-quarters of the Gulf’s daily oil output has also been derailed.
Hurricane Isaias is forcing changes ahead of the college football showdown between the University of Georgia and the Alabama Crimson Tide. CNN’s Andy Scholes breaks down what fans can expect.
From late Friday afternoon through midnight, Isaias’ dangerous conditions will begin to affect the Gulf Coast as the large storm churns northward.
Hurricane Isaias is expected to strengthen significantly over Thursday and Friday. Even if it weakens slightly before landfall, the storm will remain dangerous along the Gulf Coast.
Hurricane Isaias is due to make landfall late Friday night into Saturday as a strong Category two storm. A state of emergency has been declared across Florida and Alabama.
Meteorologist Ali Van Fleet explains how a weakening hurricane can still grow in size and threaten a broader region with rain, storm surge and even tornadoes.
All hurricanes are dangerous, but their impacts aren't always created equal. Meteorologist Chris Warren explains how storm size and storm strength influence the impacts communities experience before, during and after landfall.
To help people prepare for hurricanes, scientists studied 40 tropical cyclones and found storm surge hits in eight ways.
Hurricane Isaias’ inner core has started to move ashore along the Gulf Coast, ushering in 70+ mph winds, torrential rain and storm surge.
The center of the storm is still about 70 miles offshore, so we’re still two to three hours away from landfall, but conditions will continue to deteriorate quickly as the storm moves closer.
The number of power outages in the Gulf Coast continues to rise, now topping more than 180,000 people affected in five states.
Florida and Alabama are feeling the extreme effects of Hurricane Isaias as it is set to make landfall in a matter of hours.
Here’s the latest number of people in the dark, according to tracker PowerOutage.us .
Photojournalists in the Florida Panhandle have spent the day documenting Gulf Coast communities as they brace for Isaias’ landfall, which is now only a few hours away.
Their images show scenes of residents boarding up their homes and businesses, people heeding evacuating orders and waves churning in the Gulf as the hurricane approaches.
Alabama and Florida officials warned early in the evening it is now too dangerous to evacuate. Instead, they said people should shelter in place to wait until Isaias has passed.
“It’s too late to make any preparations. It’s probably too late to even leave,” Grant Brown, public information officer for Gulf Shores, Alabama, told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “So at this point, make sure you’re protecting yourself. Find a good place to hunker down and ride this storm out.”
Gulf Shores, like other coastal cities, is set to initiate its curfew from 7 p.m. Friday until 7 a.m. Saturday.
In Bay County, Florida, Commissioner Daniel Raffield also urged people to shelter in place.
“If you didn’t listen to the warning from the county and state, we highly encourage you not to leave,” he told Tapper. “Stay where you are. Please don’t get on the roads.”
Heavy rain and powerful winds are pummeling Pensacola Beach, Florida, according to CNN national correspondent Rafael Romo who is on the ground.
The sky is dark as Hurricane Isaias approaches the coast, with winds whipping vegetation so hard that they bend over. The wind is also picking up water off the ocean, creating mist and high waves.
People appeared to have listening to warnings from officials to take shelter. No one is on the roads or out on the street, Romo reported.
Hurricane force winds of 74 mph or greater are moving onshore as Hurricane Isaias makes its final approach toward the Gulf Coast.
According to the National Hurricane Center, a wind gust of 72 mph was recently recorded at Orange Beach in Alabama.
As of 6 p.m. ET, the storm was located 70 miles south-southeast of Pensacola, and was moving north at 17 mph.
More than 55,000 people in Alabama are without power as Hurricane Isaias is just hours away from making landfall, according to PowerOutage.us .
Most of the outages are several of the state’s southern counties, with more than 35,000 outages in Mobile County alone and another more than 15,000 in neighboring Baldwin County.
Another more than 42,000 customers are in the dark in Florida. Gov. Ron DeSantis told CNN in the last hour that there are 16,000 lineman pre-positioned to respond to those outages and restore power as fast as possible when the storm passes.
In Louisiana and Mississippi, which is also feeling the effects of the storm, thousands more are also without power.
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey has urged residents to remain vigilant as Hurricane Isaias approaches the state, bringing strong winds, heavy rain and possible tornadoes.
Downed trees and power outages are likely, Ivey added.
Alabama residents can sign up for emergency alerts from the state Emergency Management Agency by texting texting “Alalert” to 77295 or by visiting ema.alabama.gov .
Videos from Saildrone, a maritime defense company that operates ocean drones, and NOAA capture choppy waves as Hurricane Isaias moves through the Gulf of Mexico toward Florida on Friday.
Saildrone told CNN the uncrewed vessel passed through the storm’s eye to gather data for NOAA roughly 150 nautical miles south of Pensacola, Florida.
According to Saildrone, the drone sailboat, which is loaded with weather instruments, encountered winds exceeding 103 miles per hour and wave heights over 32 feet.
Conditions in Gulf Shores, Alabama, are deteriorating by the hour as Hurricane Isaias approaches. The outer bands are bringing strong, tropical storm-force winds.
Those winds are coming in from the northeast, and with the rain, it’s like getting slapped right in the face. It’s just so strong.
CNN meteorologist Brandon Miller says that this coastal community is getting 56-mile-per-hour wind gusts, and that’s only going to get worse in the hours before landfall.
For now, the winds are actually pushing the storm surge away from the coast.
Miller also said that after the eyewall passes, there will be very little rain, but these tremendous winds will stick around, with 56-mile-per-hour gusts. This is enough to topple trees and cause major power outages, and this is why Gulf Shores is taking this so seriously.
They have instituted a curfew that’s set to start in two hours. They definitely shut down the bridges leading in and out hours ago.
They don’t want people out here in these conditions.
I’ve been in so many hurricanes, but probably not as close to where they’re making landfall.
The mayor was hoping people would take this seriously, and based on everything I’ve seen, it’s a ghost town out here. I think people have gotten the message. No more time for preparation. It’s time to hunker down and ride this out.
Several concerts and music festivals have been postponed or canceled across the Southeast this weekend amid concerns of tornado threats, heavy rain, saturated grounds, flooded roads and dangerous winds from Hurricane Isaias.

articles.title_orig: World-renowned violinist Simon Zhu makes North American debut in metro Atlanta with $10 million Stradivarius
articles.title_zh: World-renowned violinist Simon Zhu makes North American debut in metro Atlanta with $10 million Stradivarius
articles.content_orig:
From Shanghai to Salzburg, classical violinist Simon Zhu has commanded stages worldwide. Now, the internationally acclaimed virtuoso is making his North American debut here in metro Atlanta.
Zhu, the winner of the prestigious Premio Paganini violin competition, is taking the stage in Sandy Springs alongside the Johns Creek Symphony Orchestra as the ensemble celebrates its milestone 20th anniversary season.
During rehearsals, Zhu commanded the room with effortless precision, playing a centuries-old Stradivarius violin valued at over $10 million. The instrument is currently on loan to him for his concert tour.
"Stradivarius is the most prolific violin maker in history," Zhu said. "We dream of playing a Stradivarius at some point in our lives. It's an Italian violin from the 1700s, and it's quite amazing to play something so historic and valuable. It's also a big responsibility. It's been an honor and a privilege to be able to play such an old and valuable instrument."
For his debut performance, Zhu is taking on Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's "Violin Concerto in D major," widely regarded as one of the most demanding and celebrated cornerstones of classical repertoire.
"I will be playing the Tchaikovsky Concerto, which is probably the most performed violin concerto in the world in classical music," Zhu said. "I just get more excited to perform it because it has these really emotional and lush melodies, but it also shows what the violin can do at a versatility level."
The concert also marks a major celebratory moment for the Johns Creek Symphony Orchestra, commemorating two decades of performing for the community.
Music Director Henry Chang curated an expansive, genre-crossing program designed to bridge classical tradition with contemporary works.
"We will start with a piece by Christopher Tin with a 100-piece choir talking about the dream of flight," Chang said, pointing to Tin's renowned crossover music heard everywhere from concert halls to major video game soundtracks.
The orchestra will also tackle Igor Stravinsky's landmark masterwork, "The Firebird."
"It is really the iconic example of rebirth through trials and fires, and it's very fitting for us as an orchestra," Chang explained. "Having come through the last 20 years of struggles, we continue with our mission to engage the community."
Chang emphasized that the evening's selections were specifically chosen to demystify orchestral music and connect directly with listeners.
"In this program, everything is relatable," Chang said. "Everything is to the heart and soul of why we make music and make art. It's about connection. It's about giving yourself fully and completely."
For Zhu, sharing this historic instrument with a live audience is about carrying history forward.
"I can't wait to share my music with Atlanta, Sandy Springs, and Georgia," Zhu said. "I hope I can perform on it for a long, long time."
To welcome the next generation of classical music fans, the Johns Creek Symphony Orchestra offered free admission for all students up to age 21 with a valid student ID.

articles.title_orig: Trump announces deal with Putin to release Russian diesel
articles.title_zh: Trump announces deal with Putin to release Russian diesel
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel to the US and globally.
Trump said the proposed release of hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel, in tranches, would see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!".
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April 2027 as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.
Ukraine's president criticised the decision, saying any easing of sanctions on Russia played into Moscow's hands and would prolong the war between the two countries.
Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.
He added that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period" after, dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have seen attacks by Ukraine.
Putin later said Russia was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.
The BBC has asked the White House for clarity on what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.
Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.
That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (Â£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.
Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
But Zelensky hit out at it, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on social media.
Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, and introduced a ban on diesel exports.
According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.
Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.
But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".
"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.
Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear.
But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.
What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.
With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.
Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.
Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

articles.title_orig: Decade-old RAM is making a comeback
articles.title_zh: Decade-old RAM is making a comeback
articles.content_orig:
The RAM shortage is bringing back DDR4, with new Intel and AMD CPUs for older RAM, sockets, and chipsets.
The RAM shortage is bringing back DDR4, with new Intel and AMD CPUs for older RAM, sockets, and chipsets.
CPU makers have noticed that the seemingly unending RAM price hikes are making it tough for a lot of us to upgrade our PCs. Their solution? A return to last-gen DDR4 RAM. Intel and AMD are making new CPUs that’ll support the older, more affordable type of memory.
On Friday, Gigabyte announced that two of its motherboard lines will support “upcoming” processors built on Intel’s LGA 1700 socket. That socket debuted in 2021 with the 12th gen Alder Lake CPUs and supported both DDR4 RAM and the then-new DDR5 RAM. Intel dropped it for a DDR5-only approach in 2024. But according to Gigabyte, the dual format support is now being revived, with new LGA 1700 chips “expected to launch in early 2027.”
Intel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
This backtrack stems from LGA 1700’s cross-compatibility with both kinds of RAM — an advantage over its successor that’s recently become much more important. Intel’s strategy may be to offer users the choice of a new CPU that doesn’t require them to switch to new, and very expensive, DDR5 memory, too. AMD is doing something similar: in August, Gigabyte also announced a new series of motherboards for AMD’s last-gen, DDR4-compatible AM4 platform to go along with the 10th-anniversary relaunch of the Ryzen 7 5800X3D CPU.
DDR4 started hitting the market in 2014 and has since been succeeded by the much faster DDR5. Under normal circumstances, buying new hardware to use technology that’s over a decade old would probably be a bad investment. But the RAM shortage is changing the math, with DDR4 RAM seemingly feeling the sting of price hikes much less than DDR5.
I recently saw the price disparity first-hand while shopping around for new RAM after a DDR4 kit abruptly died on me. Right now, a DDR5 32GB Corsair Vengeance RAM kit costs $620, while the corresponding DDR4 kit costs $260. Even though it’s more than 32GB of DDR4 RAM typically cost back in mid-2025 , that’s more than double the price for DDR5! Of course, DDR5 has significant advantages, like higher speeds and better power efficiency. But those perks might not be worth the current price of admission.
It could be years before prices drop again, a reality that’s starting to really sink in with the official return of older sockets and chipsets. But at least it’s a good time to hang onto your DDR4 RAM.

articles.title_orig: NYPD body camera video shows aftermath of ICE agent shooting man in Marble Hill
articles.title_zh: NYPD body camera video shows aftermath of ICE agent shooting man in Marble Hill
articles.content_orig:
As outrage simmers over an ICE agent shooting a man who had a 5-year-old child in a car in New York City's Marble Hill Thursday, the Department of Homeland Security is pushing back.
Oscar Bergal, 28, was shot once in the neck by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who fired shots at his car Thursday afternoon, according to authorities. The child was in the back seat, and was not struck.
Bergal's attorneys appeared in a Lower Manhattan court Friday afternoon claiming he was arrested without a valid warrant, and they are petitioning for him to be released from federal custody.
Bergal was initially taken to a detention facility in Newark but has since been moved to Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, according to his attorneys. The bullet is still in his body, and he's still in pain, his attorney said.
New surveillance video shows plainclothes agents approaching the silver car Thursday afternoon in Marble Hill. It starts to drive, when DHS said one of their agents opened fire, shooting Bergal.
The NYPD Friday released body camera footage from the first NYPD officers on the scene. The NYPD said those officers responded after the shooting, and were not involved in the shooting itself.
The video shows two officers driving up to the scene. When they exit the car, pedestrians nearby can be heard talking about how ICE agents were involved in the shooting.
Bergal can be seen sitting on the ground. A man in a reflective vest carrying a long gun can be seen standing nearby. The officers can be heard calling for an ambulance, before apparently deciding not to wait. They can then be seen on the video placing Bergal into a police vehicle, rushing him to a hospital, and carrying him to the emergency room.
"There was nothing that was happening that would make people have to disguise themselves as construction workers, surround a man's car with his 5-year-old son in it, coming from school at 4 o'clock in the afternoon, and shoot him in the neck in the car," Public Advocate Jumaane Williams said.
DHS defended the shooting at a news conference Friday morning.
"This individual yesterday decided to not comply with lawful orders given by federal law enforcement officers, ICE officers. Good men and women that are out there every day enforcing immigration laws," Marcos Charles of ICE said.
DHS said Bergal was in the U.S. illegally and was the object of a targeted enforcement operation. Bergal had alleged associations with the Trinitarios gang and had a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, and weapons possession.
Court documents show Bergal was arrested in August 2025 for selling cocaine and fentanyl in Manhattan. The special narcotics prosecutor's office says he had been let out on supervised release.
DHS claims agents tried to detain Bergal in September unsuccessfully, before pursuing him Thursday.
"Mr. Bergal refused lawful orders to exit his vehicle. He then accelerated his vehicle, smashing into two of our government ICE vehicles, and then weaponized his vehicle and proceeded to accelerate going toward other officers," Charles said.
Ruth Hilaria, who works at a deli nearby the site of the shooting,  told CBS News New York that's not what she saw. She said the car was driving away from the ICE agents.
"All I can say at this point is, regardless of whether or not someone has a criminal history, it is not lawful and it is not OK to shoot a father in the afternoon with his son in the back seat," Bergal's attorney Howard Solis said.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he tried unsuccessfully to negotiate with President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin last night for Bergal's release.
"President Trump actually got involved and said that we would release him to New York's Finest. If NYPD wants to take the charges and pursue the charges, we'll be happy to release him into the custody of NYPD. I shared that with the mayor. The mayor once again said we will not be detaining him," Mullin said.
CBS News New York has asked City Hall for comment on Mullin's claim and has not yet heard back.
DHS said the agent did not know Bergal's 5-year-old son was in the back seat of the car when he opened fire.
Hilaria said she heard the boy crying out for his father after the shooting.
Rep. Adriano Espaillat visited the boy later at the hospital.
"He was watching cartoons on TV," Espaillat said. "I just gave him high five, and we had a nice conversation, and he seemed to be physically in good shape. But the mom told me that he was very afraid and kept repeating what occurred."
"That child is terrorized. Usually a very chatty, talkative child, very carefree. The mom says he just won't talk. He's just traumatized," Gov. Kathy Hochul said.
Meanwhile, multiple officials are calling for an investigation into the shooting, as well as for an end to ICE activities in New York.
"We have insisted the body cam footage be released to the public as soon as possible. This is exactly what I told the president last night," Hochul said. "I want a cessation of ICE activities in New York, at least in the short term. Let us calm everything down. I said, this is a tinderbox."
"Late yesterday afternoon, an ICE officer shot a New Yorker in his car while a five-year-old child sat in the backseat. I am praying for the victim and his loved ones, and I am praying for the continued safety of the young child who, only by the grace of God, was not physically harmed," New York Attorney General Letitia James said. "Today, New Yorkers are grappling with horror and outrage. They deserve nothing less than a full and transparent investigation conducted without fear or favor. I have full faith in District Attorney [Bronx DA] Darcel Clark."
"My office is working to establish facts and determine the appropriate course of action," Clark said. "We will continue to conduct a thorough investigation where our process is guided by the evidence and the law."
Bergal's shooting prompted almost immediate protests and condemnation from elected officials, including Mamdani .
"New York City will not stand by while ICE agents shoot New Yorkers. And we will not back down from the demand that so many, including myself, have put forward time and again. This is an agency that must be abolished," Mamdani said Thursday night.
Five people were taken into custody amid Thursday night's protests. Another protest is scheduled for Friday evening in Lower Manhattan.
Editor's note 10/9/26 3:56 p.m.: Authorities initially said the last name of the man who was shot was Belgal. Authorities have since said his last name is Bergal. This story has been updated to reflect that change.

articles.title_orig: Two powerful earthquakes and multiple aftershocks rock Panama
articles.title_zh: Two powerful earthquakes and multiple aftershocks rock Panama
articles.content_orig:
A major earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.7 has struck southern Panama, according to the US Geological Survey.
Several people have suffered minor injuries but so far there are no reports of fatalities or missing persons, officials said. Various homes, roads, hotels, government buildings, businesses and churches have sustained structural damage, according to the civil protection system.
The USGS had said some casualties were possible and extensive damage was probable.
Footage verified by CNN shows several damaged buildings in Penonome, some 70 miles from the epicenter. One video shows a church with a partially collapsed steeple and another building with a crumbled facade.
In the popular resort town Playa Venao, a multi-story building collapsed and crushed several cars beneath it.
Along the Panama Canal, the Centennial Bridge’s suspension cables were seen shaking as vehicles drove through.
The canal’s authority said operations were continuing as normal and that staff were inspecting facilities for potential damage.
Panama City’s public transit system has suspended service on two metro lines and evacuated passengers from some stations.
Scores of residents gathered in the streets of the capital after rushing out of their buildings in a panic.
“I am on the ninth floor here and yes it was felt strongly, it was felt strongly,” Panama City resident Kevin Cortez told Reuters.
“Everything was moving: the lamp, the chair, the table,” another resident said. “I decided to stay and wait because I knew running down the stairs was a problem. So I stayed waiting for it to pass. I had no other option. Yes, we felt it was quite prolonged. People running, shouting; not everyone takes it the same way, but well, here we are, downstairs.”
The Education Ministry has canceled classes nationwide for the rest of the day.
Panama’s main international airport was temporarily closed as a precaution and flights were diverted to other airports before operations resumed later in the day, the civil aviation authority said.
The water and sewage institute has reported interruptions at several water treatment plants due to power outages caused by the quake.
Panama’s President José Raúl Mulino has called for calm and instructed the minister of government to provide information on the earthquake’s effects. He has also mobilized resources to those affected.
Mulino visited an affected hospital in Penonome, where several patients were evacuated and have had to receive treatment outdoors.
Officials have reported more than 40 aftershocks, including one with a preliminary magnitude of 6.6, according to USGS.
Earlier, the US Tsunami Warning System warned of possible tsunami waves along some coasts before saying there was no longer a threat.
This is the latest powerful earthquake to have struck Latin America this year. Over the summer, Venezuela was hit by two powerful earthquakes that killed more than 6,400 people, while Colombia suffered a tremor that left around 300 dead.
The leaders of both countries have offered to help Panama’s government as it responds to the disaster.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Houthi attack on Riyadh airport killed three Saudi nationals
articles.title_zh: Houthi attack on Riyadh airport killed three Saudi nationals
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia has said that three people including a pilot were killed in Thursday’s Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
In a statement on social media on Friday, the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said attacks on the airport killed an airline pilot and two other Saudi citizens, while several people “of different nationalities were wounded”.
“It is with profound sadness that Saudia announces the passing of Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami,” the flag-carrier said in a statement, citing an “incident” at the Riyadh airport.
Dozens of people wounded in the missile attacks suffered minor to severe injuries. The attacks also caused material damage, including to a plane operated by national carrier Saudia, GACA said. Airport operations have now resumed and air traffic has returned to normal, according to Saudi media reports.
Saudi Arabia has seen several attacks by the Houthis in recent days, with the airports appearing to be the primary target.
GACA said Wednesday that attacks earlier in the week had killed three civilians and injured 36 at Abha and King Khalid airports. At least three people were also wounded in other attacks on Jazan and Najran airports near the Yemen border.
A Houthi military spokesperson said on Thursday that the armed group had launched a ballistic missile towards King Khalid Airport, claiming that the missile had successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic.
The Houthi military campaign appears to be a revival of a tactic seen last month. On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards King Khalid airport. A day later, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area.
The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there, except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, is a target.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa in Yemen, said the Houthis want to impose a blockade on all Saudi airports.
“This is part of the blockade-for-blockade equation, the airport-for-airport equation. Because Sanaa remains besieged by Saudi Arabia, the Ansar Allah Houthis want to impose a blockade on all Saudi airports”, Mawry said.
The Houthis say the strikes are in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen’s Sanaa International Airport and the airport in Hodeidah, he said.
The resumption of attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports comes as Yemeni forces continue a counteroffensive against the Houthis.
Late on Friday, air strikes were reported in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which remains under the control of the Houthi movement, which seized the city in 2014.
Loud explosions were also reported in the southern port city of Aden, where the internationally-recognised Yemeni government is based.
The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government also said on Friday that it had destroyed three rocket launch platforms that were used by the Houthis “to threaten regional security”.
Coalition spokesman Colonel Turki al-Maliki declared that all Houthi attacks on civilians and civilian facilities “will be met with resolve” by the Saudi-led coalition.
The push by Yemeni forces and the Saudi-led coalition was launched after the Iran-aligned rebel group last month seized a broad swath of territory in Yemen along the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, in a sudden push.
Yemeni government forces this week claimed key gains around the Bab al-Mandeb coastline, but intense fighting continues.
The conflict, which was frozen for years but reignited after the United States and Israel’s war on Iran, has stoked further upheaval in a region already destabilised by Israel’s wars on Gaza and Lebanon.
It now threatens to draw other states into the conflict, with Pakistan and Turkiye having agreed to deploy troops under a mutual defence pact signed with Saudi Arabia earlier this year.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan said on Friday that the country now has a “substantial number of forces as well as resources … in Riyadh”.
Pakistani military personnel “would not be crossing the borders of the other side for an attack on the Houthis, but of course [are acting] in the defence of the territory”, he noted.
Meanwhile, at the United Nations on Friday, Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia asked the Security Council to take action to address the escalating situation in Yemen.
“The increasing targeting of civilians, the continuing threats to the security of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and the resulting repercussions that extend beyond Yemen and the region negatively affect international peace and security,” Saudi Arabia’s UN representative, Abdulaziz al-Wasil, told the council.
Abdullah Ali Fadhel al-Saadi, the UN representative for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, said that the threat posed by the Houthis, “is no longer an internal Yemeni affair that can be contained within our borders”.
