articles.title_orig: CISA, FBI, NSA Flag China's Integrity Tech Cyber Threat
articles.title_zh: CISA, FBI, NSA Flag China's Integrity Tech Cyber Threat
articles.content_orig:
Photo: KanawatTH/Adobe Stock
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the National Security Agency and foreign partners have released a joint cybersecurity advisory identifying Integrity Technology Group, a Chinese cybersecurity firm, as a facilitator of hacking campaigns against critical infrastructure organizations worldwide .
CISA said Thursday the guidance draws on investigations and activity seen in Africa, North America and Southeast Asia.
CISA’s Acting Associate Director for Threat Hunting Bobby Thompson will be among the keynote speakers at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Homeland Security Summit on Nov. 10, wherein Department of Homeland Security leaders and industry together will discuss the strategic DHS priorities. Register today to hear from government decision-makers through keynotes, panels and Q&A sessions.
According to the advisory, Integrity Tech, which the agencies tie to the Chinese government, procures and builds cyber tools, hosts infrastructure and breaches networks globally. Actors it supports rely on living-off-the-land techniques, large botnets and virtual private network infrastructure. Their methods mirror tradecraft publicly tracked as Red Juliett, Flax Typhoon and Ethereal Panda.
The advisory says the actors struck government, critical manufacturing and healthcare entities, along with U.S. law enforcement agencies and education institutions. To keep stealthy, persistent footholds, they have focused on edge devices that victims seldom monitor closely.
The agencies are urging all organizations, particularly critical infrastructure operators, to review the guidance, hunt for indicators of compromise and apply its mitigations. Those include hardening edge infrastructure and patching common vulnerabilities and exposures, or CVEs, that adversaries have already exploited.
Chris Butera , CISA’s acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity, said actors affiliated with Beijing are embedding themselves in critical infrastructure, including operational technology systems, “with the aim of disrupting critical functions at a future time of their choosing.”
Brett Leatherman , assistant director of the FBI Cyber Division, said the bureau’s cyber strategy targets both threat actors and “the enterprises that support them.” He called on organizations to flag suspicious activity to their nearest FBI field office.
In August, NSA, the FBI and the Cyber National Mission Force warned of QTFY , a China-linked hacking group, as the Justice Department seized domains tied to its tools. In April, CISA and the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre detailed how Volt Typhoon and Flax Typhoon build covert networks from compromised routers and internet-of-things devices. In September, the three agencies highlighted Chinese AI firms’ distillation campaigns against U.S. frontier models.
The warning follows the White House’s March release of its Cyber Strategy for America and the Department of War’s 2026 National Defense Strategy , which prioritizes homeland cyber defense.

articles.title_orig: James Talarico back on the trail after an absence with the flu drew scrutiny
articles.title_zh: James Talarico back on the trail after an absence with the flu drew scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
After drawing scrutiny for his absence from the campaign trail, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, who had been sick with the flu, returned to the stump in Texas on Friday.
“James Talarico is back on the campaign trail talking to voters at Austin City Limits,” Talarico campaign spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement.
Social media posts showed Talarico walking on the grounds of the festival on Friday.
Talarico revealed on Sept. 30 that he was sick, when he had to appear virtually instead of in person at a forum. His prolonged absence drew daily scrutiny from his opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Paxton’s campaign asked for “proof of life” and called on Talarico to produce a photo of himself and a newspaper with a current date. Republican Sen. Ted Cruz poked fun on social media, featuring a milk carton with Talarico’s face with the word “MISSING.”
Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser and, according to his virtual remarks to the Hispanic Business Council the following day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care.
Then, Talarico appeared visibly ill, blowing his nose and coughing through the event.
“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.”
His absence from the trail in the crunch time of the election prompted some consternation among Democrats.
“Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said . “We’d rather have him on the trail.”
Natasha Korecki is a senior national political reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: How Well Do AI Risk Estimates Match Real-World Prostate Cancer Outcomes?
articles.title_zh: How Well Do AI Risk Estimates Match Real-World Prostate Cancer Outcomes?
articles.content_orig:
Daniel Spratt, MD, reviews how closely MMAI-predicted 10-year distant metastasis and prostate cancer–specific mortality tracked observed STAR-CAP outcomes, including among patients treated with surgery.
Daniel Spratt, MD, describes the core findings of the benchmarking analysis. 1 For 10-year distant metastasis, he says, the MMAI-predicted risk estimates from a real-world commercial cohort were strikingly similar to the outcomes actually observed in STAR-CAP across National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) low-, intermediate-, and high-risk disease, differing on the order of approximately 1%, with confidence intervals around both estimates. In the data presented, MMAI predicted 10-year distant metastasis rates of 2.4%, 3.4%, and 12.9% for NCCN low-, intermediate-, and high-risk disease, compared with observed rates of 1.0%, 4.0%, and 13.5% in STAR-CAP. Spratt notes the agreement is notable given that some STAR-CAP patients were treated in a more historical era.
He then turns to prostate cancer–specific mortality (PCSM), an outcome he says patients want to understand, particularly with more aggressive disease, because a reduction in metastasis that does not change survival is an important distinction to discuss. Here, too, Spratt reports strong concordance between predicted and observed outcomes. MMAI predicted 10-year PCSM of 1.1%, 1.6%, and 6.7% for NCCN low-, intermediate-, and high-risk disease, vs observed rates of 0.5%, 2.0%, and 8.2%; the analysis also compared PCSM across STAR-CAP stage groups.
Spratt also addresses a common concern. MMAI was initially validated in randomized trials of patients treated with radiotherapy with or without hormone therapy, raising questions about patients who choose surgery. The majority of STAR-CAP patients underwent surgery, he explains, and calibration remained accurate in this mixed surgery and radiation cohort, consistent with the principle that a prognostic tool should perform regardless of the treatment a patient receives.
In the next segment, Spratt walks through how he weighs MMAI results alongside NCCN risk groups, including when the two point in opposite directions.

articles.content_orig:
Attorneys representing Winston Lee, one of the former fraternity members accused in the Cornell University sexual assault lawsuit , filed a motion Friday in criminal court seeking to disqualify New York Attorney General Letitia James from any future grand jury proceedings.
The motion — filed by attorneys Teny Geragos, Marc Agnifilo and Jacob Kaplan — asked a judge to preclude James from conducting a criminal investigation into whether former Chi Phi members, including Lee, engaged in sexual assault in October 2024.
Lee’s attorneys argued that the Tompkins County court has the authority to step in if necessary to ensure the fairness of a grand jury process. They are asking for any future potential grand jury panelists to be polled on whether they are aware of James’ comments. They also asked for the court to schedule arguments on the issue.
In response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for James’ office said: “In this and every investigation, the Office of the Attorney General is committed to conducting a comprehensive review of nothing but the facts, the evidence, and the law.”
The filing follows a separate legal effort by lawyers for Cornell defendant Gillio Lopes , who earlier this week filed a civil court motion asking a judge for the same relief: the dismissal of James following her appointment as special counsel by Gov. Kathy Hochul.
Jane Doe’s civil suit was filed last month against seven fraternity members as well as Cornell, the Chi Phi fraternity and her sorority. The lawsuit alleges that both Lee and Lopes did drugs off her body and sexually assaulted her. Lee’s and Lopes’ attorneys say their clients deny the accusations brought against them.
Two of the other men named in the suit have also denied separate allegations against them. None of the men named has been criminally charged. Cornell has said that it welcomes new investigations into the case. The fraternity and sorority previously declined to discuss the pending litigation.
It also marks the first time the well-known legal team, which has handled a number of significant sexual misconduct matters, publicly acknowledged representing one of the men accused by a former Cornell student who filed a lawsuit last month under the pseudonym Jane Doe.
Hochul and James “have together created a blatant appearance of impropriety that, combined with the AG’s ethical violations, should lead to the AG’s recusal,” Geragos wrote in a motion filed in criminal court in Tompkins County, the upstate New York area where Cornell is located.
Geragos pointed to social media comments posted by James as Jane Doe’s lawsuit captured national attention.
“What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable,” James wrote prior to her appointment as special prosecutor. “To her and all other survivors: You’re not alone. We stand with you.”
Lawyers for Lee and Lopes argue the remarks show that James prejudged the case and is unfit to conduct an impartial review of the matter. An Oct. 29 hearing has been set in Lopes’ case for James’ office to argue that her appointment should not be voided.
“The public needs confidence that the person directing this investigation will evaluate the evidence with an open mind,” Lopes’ attorney, Andrew Miltenberg, said in a statement on Friday.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten vowed to present evidence to a grand jury prior to James’ office taking on the probe.
Van Houten previously found that Jane Doe had not described a prosecutable crime in a six-page statement provided to police in November 2024 and ruled out the possibility of charges. Jane Doe told police that she engaged in a consensual threesome on the evening in question, but that events spiraled as she became increasingly incapacitated and more men became involved.
Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for Jane Doe, has previously said that sex assault victims sometimes do not immediately recognize the coercive nature of an encounter because they rationalize aspects of a traumatic event.
Geragos’ law firm, Agnifilo Intrater LLP, previously represented hip-hop mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs and Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein in high-profile criminal trials.
Combs, 56, was acquitted in July 2025 on one count of racketeering conspiracy and two counts of sex trafficking by force, fraud or coercion. The jury found him guilty on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. The rapper and record producer was sentenced to 50 months in federal prison .
The jury in Weinstein’s third trial failed to reach a unanimous verdict on a third-degree rape charge involving Jessica Mann, a former aspiring actor. The judge declared a mistrial in May.
In a separate trial last year, the former Miramax chief was convicted on a count of first-degree criminal sexual act involving Miriam “Mimi” Haley, a former “Project Runway” production assistant. He was recently sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Marc Agnifilo and his wife, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, represent Luigi Mangione, the 28-year-old accused of fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. Mangione in August pleaded not guilty to federal stalking charges, kicking off a double jeopardy fight in New York state court, where he still faces murder charges.

articles.title_orig: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocks Panama
articles.title_zh: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocks Panama
articles.content_orig:
A 7.7-magnitude earthquake shook the central coast of Panama on Friday, prompting tsunami warnings for several neighboring countries.
The earthquake hit around 1:56 p.m. ET, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Around three hours later, a second powerful earthquake measuring at 6.6 magnitude, struck Panama after a series of aftershocks, which registered magnitudes between 4.8 and 5.8, rippled across the southern tip of the country.
Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt.
The U.S. Tsunami Center flagged tsunami warnings for Ecuador, Colombia, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Mexico, El Salvador, Costa Rica and Peru, as well as Panama, shortly after the quake.
The initial earthquake was centered about 6 miles southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama’s southern tip, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 6 miles.
Tremors were also felt in the capital, Panama City , where buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets. The city is known for its tall skyscrapers.
Visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.
“We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re OK, though we’re very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.”
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.
Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square and the Dos Continentes hotel.
No casualties were immediately reported, but Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of Panama Civil Protection said injured people “have been transferred to educational centers, health centers, and hospital centers.”
The province of Coclé said the governor’s palace there suffered significant structural damage, but that staff members were safely evacuated. The local government also urged community members to remain calm in the quake’s aftermath.
Video aired by local news outlets showed a Catholic cathedral collapsing and part of a hotel’s facade falling onto a car in the city of Penonomé, in the central province of Coclé.
Social media videos show collapsed buildings near the site of the original quake and the aftershocks, including a hotel reduced to rubble in the tourist-friendly Playa Venao.
Panama’s National System for Civil Protection said it is monitoring for further reports of damage throughout the country.
Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.
Nearby countries sent messages of support Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella , whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.”
“Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” he wrote on X.
The U.S. Embassy in Panama said it was “closely monitoring” the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.
Michelle Garcia is a senior editor for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Alberta woman, 61, breaks her own world record by planking for 5 hours
articles.title_zh: Alberta woman, 61, breaks her own world record by planking for 5 hours
articles.content_orig:
You can accomplish a lot in five hours.
Fly direct from Toronto to Vancouver, for instance. Or play an entire 18-hole round of golf. Run a full marathon at an average pace. Smoke a rack of ribs.
It's an objectively long stretch of time. Now, imagine holding a plank, one of the most notoriously challenging core exercises, for the amount of time it takes to cook a Thanksgiving turkey?
"I just love it," laughed DonnaJean Wilde, who at age 61 just broke her own world record for the longest time holding an abdominal plank position (female) during the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah this week.
Wilde is a grandmother of 12 and retired teacher from Welling, Alta. And on Tuesday, in front of a cheering crowd and several judges, she held an abdominal plank for five straight hours, shattering her previous 2024 world record of four hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds.
Canadian woman holds plank for 5 hours, breaking world record
On Friday, she told CBC News Network she was "feeling good" and waiting for Guinness to make the record official.
"It just becomes easier to do the more repeated times you do it," Wilde said.
An abdominal plank is an isometric core exercise where you hold your body straight like a plank of wood. Most adults can hold a plank for 20 to 60 seconds, according to Health magazine .
Guinness World Records notes that to successfully achieve the record, the challenger's forearms and toes must touch the ground at all times. "The remainder of the body must be lifted off the ground and be kept straight throughout."
Wilde says she started planking about 15 years ago when she broke her arm and was looking for a way to stay fit.
"I love to work out. I love fitness, and I discovered I could plank with a cast on," she said.
Walk fast, live longer? McMaster University researchers say walking speed is an important health indicator
Fitness influencer apologizes after hitching a bike ride in the Berlin Marathon
"And when the cast came off, it became a habit that I actually embraced and fell in love with."
When she first started, she says she could hold a plank for about a minute or minute and a half, but she kept practicing. With her family's encouragement, she kept going and minutes became hours. By 2024, she broke the Guinness World Record.
Wilde, seen in the midst of achieving her latest world record, says that while she holds her hours-long planks she likes to multitask: reading, writing and earning her master's. (Submitted by DonnaJean Wilde)
And, for good measure, she broke a second one that year by completing 1,575 pushups in one hour — the most push ups in one hour (female) . She told the Guinness World Records she fell in love with doing pushups while doing 500 every day as training for her planks.
Now, she planks every day for at least a few hours. But it doesn't eat into her time, she says. She multitasks.
"Just read, do texts, whatever, do schoolwork. I did a master's degree while I was planking. Wrote a book," she said.
The book, From Minutes To Hours: I Wrote This Book While Planking , came out last year.
CBC News did not attempt to write this story while planking.

She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. articles.title_orig: Elon Musk’s growing SpaceX empire sends AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile shares plunging
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk’s growing SpaceX empire sends AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile shares plunging
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk’s plan for SpaceX to “become a major mobile carrier in the U.S.” sent shares of the nation’s big three wireless carriers sliding by double digits Friday, wiping out more than $50 billion in market value before lunch.
“Once we receive final FCC approval, Starlink Mobile will deploy a flexible architecture combining our satellite-to-mobile constellation in space with an advanced terrestrial deployment that can seamlessly connect devices everywhere,” the company said late Thursday.
It also announced that the Federal Communications Commission had approved the launch of 15,000 new satellites, also under Starlink Mobile, which is a subsidiary of SpaceX.
Shares of AT&T fell 9.8%, Verizon dropped 8.7%, while T-Mobile US plunged 13.3%. For Verizon, today’s performance was its worst-one day drop since 2002. It was T-Mobile’s worst day since 2011.
Shares of Charter and of Comcast, the parent company of NBC News, also fell Friday. Both companies sell wireless services under their own brands using Verizon’s infrastructure.
The announcement from SpaceX marked Musk’s latest step to expand his global tech empire. The world’s richest man and its first-ever trillionaire , Musk’s net worth as of Thursday was about $990 billion.
Musk’s constellation of companies already includes electric vehicle maker Tesla, the social media site X and xAI, which builds data centers and develops artificial intelligence.
SpaceX includes multiple lines of business, too. Starlink sells high-speed internet to companies and consumers worldwide, while Starshield does the same, but to governments.
But the major money maker for SpaceX is Starlink, which was worth $2.2 trillion as of Friday.
With more than 12 million paying subscribers, Starlink is also the only profitable part of SpaceX’s business, according to its latest earnings report.
The acquisition of spectrum was “the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk wrote on n X.
SpaceX is also a massive U.S. government contractor, building and launching rockets on behalf of NASA and several national security agencies.
Favorable decisions by government regulators and additional agency contracts are crucial to maintaining SpaceX’s lofty valuation.
As a close ally of President Donald Trump and a major donor to his 2024 election effort, Musk is a frequent guest at White House events.
At a recent White House state dinner for China’s President Xi Jinping, Musk was seated next to first lady Melania Trump.
Just this week, Trump gave Musk an award for achievements in science.
As Republicans struggle to hold on to control of the House and Senate in November’s midterm elections, Musk is once again giving tens of millions of dollars to help them.
As of Friday, Musk’s America PAC had spent more than $36 million to boost Trump’s fellow Republicans in key battleground races , according to figures compiled by Wired and verified by NBC News.
Musk also appears to have support for his deal already from FCC chairman Brendan Carr.
“All of this is going to be really good news for the American consumer,” Carr said Friday morning on CNBC .
Wall Street analysts and Starlink’s potential competitors were skeptical Friday of the SpaceX plan.
Absent a deal with an existing wireless carrier, “SpaceX would likely need to build a terrestrial network using macro towers to deliver a user experience on par with traditional wireless carriers,” wrote analysts at JPMorgan Chase.
“We continue to see limited near-term risk to U.S. wireless incumbents given the time, infrastructure and capital required to build a competitive terrestrial network,” they added.
Put another way, the analysts think SpaceX plan’s does not pose an imminent threat to the established carriers because it takes a lot more than just satellites to deliver reliable wireless service.
SpaceX would need earth-based infrastructure to bolster its network of satellites because the radio waves it purchased would likely be unable to reach the interior of some buildings, wrote analysts at UBS. “We still believe it will take time for SpaceX to scale its wireless ambitions.”
Like the analysts, the major telecom companies feeling the sting from Musk’s announcement also downplayed any risk that Starlink might pose to their businesses.
“Acquisition of spectrum alone does not provide the network or infrastructure to offer true nationwide coverage or to compete with mobile providers,” Verizon said in a statement to NBC News. “A company can have billions of dollars of spectrum, but if they do not have the network to use it, it’s just empty airwaves.”
John Saw, president of technology at T-Mobile wrote, “I have tremendous respect for what SpaceX has accomplished in space,” but that building a network would take “years of engineering.”
“You can acquire spectrum in a single transaction. You cannot acquire a nationwide, high-performing wireless network overnight,” he wrote on LinkedIn .
AT&T did not respond to a request for comment on Friday.
The three big wireless companies have a complicated relationship with Starlink. In 2022, T-Mobile announced a partnership with SpaceX, but recently dropped the name of the company from parts of its website.
And when the three wireless companies announced a joint venture recently to “eliminate coverage ‘dead zones’ and expand satellite coverage,” there was no mention of SpaceX or Starlink.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

TUSCALOOSA, Ala. ( WBRC ) - As Hurricane Isaias remains on track for a potential Alabama landfall late Friday, the University of Alabama announced Wednesday that ESPN’s College GameDay is moving indoors.
The weekly pregame show will take place inside UA’s Coleman Coliseum from 8-11 a.m. and will feature a familiar face as guest picker.
Pat McAfee announced on The Pat McAfee Show Wednesday morning that Heisman Trophy winner Bryce Young will serve as GameDay’s guest picker Saturday morning.
In recent years, College GameDay has aired from The Quad on UA’s campus. The move to Coleman Coliseum comes as Isaias strengthened overnight into a Category 2 storm.
ESPN told WBRC Tuesday that only severe weather would force College GameDay to change its plans.
University officials said there will be no overnight camping allowed and that fans can begin lining up at the north and east doors of Coleman at 5:15 a.m. Doors will open at 5:30 a.m.
A clear bag policy will be in effect for fans attending College GameDay and they will be inspected as they enter the building.
Raffle tickets for Pat McAfee’s “Kicking is Easy” contest will be distributed at both entrances, with no tickets given out before 5:15 a.m.
Fans attending College GameDay and Saturday’s Alabama-Georgia game are encouraged to monitor weather conditions and visit @UA_Athletics and @UAGameday for the most up-to-date information from the University of Alabama.

articles.title_orig: Ticker: EU and China strike interim trade deal; Trump aims at Cook, again
articles.title_zh: Ticker: EU and China strike interim trade deal; Trump aims at Cook, again
articles.content_orig:
The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said.
Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains.
The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation. The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU.
He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.”
President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn’t be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.
Trump’s extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve’s independence.

articles.title_orig: China denies report of reciprocal nuclear site visits with US
articles.title_zh: China denies report of reciprocal nuclear site visits with US
articles.content_orig:
China on Friday denied a report that Beijing and Washington had discussed reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities, with further talks reportedly planned in the coming months.
"The relevant report is not true," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular news conference in Beijing, according to an official transcript of the briefing.
The denial came after CNN reported, citing sources familiar with the matter, that China and the US had discussed possible reciprocal visits to nuclear sites.
According to an earlier CNN report, preliminary discussions covered possible visits to US Department of Energy laboratories and corresponding Chinese research centers, alongside potential access to nuclear test sites.
The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), in its June report, estimated that China possessed 620 nuclear warheads as of January 2026, compared with more than 5,000 held by the US, including retired warheads.
According to SIPRI, the world's nine nuclear-armed nations possessed an estimated 12,187 warheads, including 190 held by India, 170 by Pakistan, 90 by Israel and 60 by North Korea. Russia and the US together accounted for nearly 86% of the global inventory.
SIPRI said China was expanding its nuclear arsenal faster than any other country, while Washington and Moscow continued extensive nuclear modernization programs.
The developments follow the expiration of the New START nuclear arms reduction treaty between Washington and Moscow in February.

articles.title_orig: At 61 Years Old, This Grandmother of 12 Broke Her Own World Record With a 5-Hour Plank
articles.title_zh: At 61 Years Old, This Grandmother of 12 Broke Her Own World Record With a 5-Hour Plank
articles.content_orig:
Holiday Spending 101: Expert Tips for Saving on Gifts, Travel, More
A 61-year-old grandmother from Canada has wowed the internet by breaking her own Guinness World Record for longest time planking after holding the position for five hours.
DonnaJean Wilde of Welling, Alberta, helped kick off the Oct. 6 opening ceremonies at the Huntsman World Senior Games in St. George, Utah, when she planked in front of a crowd to beat her 2024 world record, for females, of 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds.
Viral videos from the games, which celebrate athletes ages 50 and over, show Wilde planking on a platform with a smile on her face. One video has racked up more than 9 million views with commenters expressing their awe over Wilde’s feat.
“I feel really good about it,” Wilde tells TODAY.com about her new world record. “Now that it’s done, I’m really happy.”
The retired schoolteacher said she’d wondered for a long time if she could plank for five hours straight. She began training six months ago by planking between four and five hours every day.
On Tuesday, she began her record-breaking plank with confidence, but shortly after she surpassed her record 2024 time, she began losing steam.
“That last half hour was harder than I ever thought it would be, I think I just kind of hit a wall,” Wilde says.
It was the crowd chanting her name that helped her get the job done.
“The crowd was cheering through the last few minutes and they carried me through,” she says. “And now I look back and I think, ‘Wow, wow, we did it. We did it together.’”
The mom of five, who also holds a second Guinness World Record for most pushups in one hour by a female — she did 1575 of them in just under 60 minutes in 2024 — tells TODAY.com she fell in love with sports and fitness as a child.
A lifelong runner, Wilde ran track in junior high and high school. She began planking 15 years ago after breaking her wrist in a gym accident.
“I had a cast on and I couldn’t run. I couldn’t work out. I couldn’t do everything I wanted to do, and then I discovered planking,” Wilde recalls.
At first, Wilde could hold the position only for a minute or two. She figured she’d keep at it until her cast came off and then return to her regular exercises.
Instead, she “fell in love” with planking.
“I just kept doing it and doing it ... so I planned my school lessons and marked my students’ work while I was planking,” says Wilde.
For years now, Wilde has planked for about two hours every day, incorporating the low-impact exercise into other tasks.
“I go on the floor and plank when I have something I need to do, like texting, emailing, reading or messaging somebody,” Wilde says, adding she also planks while doing an assignment or calling one of her kids.
If Wilde’s husband Randy, 63, also a fitness enthusiast, turns on a movie, Wilde will watch it with him while on the floor planking.
The physical benefits of planking can’t be beat.
Planking helps tone all of the muscle groups, including abs , arms, back, shoulders , glutes and legs, experts say. Planking can also help improve balance, ease back pain and reduce belly fat.
“Planking makes me feel so good and helps me stand up straight,” says Wilde.
Asked how strong her core muscles are, Wilde simply laughs.
Wilde and her husband stay healthy by walking or running together every day. They also work out in their home gym.
The couple’s kids and 12 grandkids have inherited their love of sports and fitness.
“Ten out of 12 grandchildren at this moment are on at least one or two sports teams, like volleyball, basketball, baseball, football. The two who aren’t on sports teams are into dancing and gymnastics,” Wilde says.
As for Wilde’s diet, she shares that she and Randy try to stick to fresh whole foods.
“Lots of eggs, lots of real protein, lots of real fruits and vegetables, oatmeal, just real food,” Wilde says.
“If we go somewhere, of course, then we will eat whatever anybody serves us. We don’t worry about it,” she adds.
Does Wilde foresee herself attempting to break her world record for planking again in the future?
“I’m not sure I’m going to try and break my planking record. Maybe my push-up record,” Wilde says, laughing.
Gina Vivinetto is a trending news reporter for TODAY.com

articles.title_orig: President Donald Trump cancels plans to attend Georgia vs. Alabama due to Hurricane Isaias
articles.title_zh: President Donald Trump cancels plans to attend Georgia vs. Alabama due to Hurricane Isaias
articles.content_orig:
Hurricanes Isaias has affected travel plans around the country, and that includes President Donald Trump. Originally, Trump planned to be in attendance when No. 2 Georgia faced No. 6 Alabama in Bryant-Denny Stadium on Saturday, but the Tuscaloosa Police Department told AL.com that he scrapped the trip due to the impending storm.
Trump has attended several Alabama football games throughout his tenure, and he's friendly with legendary coach Nick Saban, who has expressed support for Trump as it pertains to the Protect College Sports Act.
In 2018, Trump made the trip down to Atlanta for the College Playoff National Championship, which the Crimson Tide won due to overtime heroics from Tua Tagovailoa. The next year, in 2019, Trump was at Bryant-Denny Stadium for the shootout that was LSU vs. Alabama.
While weather may have nixed this trip, Trump has gotten to watch a little college football in person this season. He was in Knoxville just two weeks ago when Texas triumphed over Tennessee , 20-17.
For the moment, Hurricanes Isaias isn't expected to change much about the game itself. Both teams are planning to play on Saturday night in Tuscaloosa as scheduled, but the SEC is monitoring the storm and the kickoff time could be altered slightly.
The storm is expected to bring locally heavy rain, potential flooding, high winds and isolated tornadoes throughout the Southeast this weekend, although the exact path is still unknown.
According to both coaches, the teams are preparing as normal for the game, since the weather is well outside of their control. Wet-ball drills and mental preparation are all that can be done for now.
"Depends on the level of weather you get, it would affect what happens," Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer said, according to 247Sports . "It's just -- that's not my area of expertise. I'm just getting our football team ready. It hasn't affected us much, other than we're doing wet ball drills and get wet ball involved in some of our team reps, just like we did last week at times, preparing for the rain a week ago. I'm not really involved in too much."

articles.title_orig: Here’s how Treasury yields could rise to 6% — even without market upheaval
articles.title_zh: Here’s how Treasury yields could rise to 6% — even without market upheaval
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
(Bloomberg) -- It's one of the least understood signals in the fixed-income world, but lately, everyone on Wall Street is abuzz about what it means as it reasserts itself in the market.
US Bars Microsoft, Indian Firms From Visa Program in Blow
UPS Worker Missed Email, Letting China Get F-35 Parts
India Scraps Key Tax Relief on Gold Imports, Raising Costs
Reliance May Be a Cheaper Way to Buy Jio After Its Listing
Apple to Launch Doorbell, Lock, Thermostat Developed With LG
It's known as the term premium, or the extra payout that investors demand in return for the risks of owning 10-year Treasuries instead of just rolling over short-dated securities for the same amount of time. How exactly to measure it varies. So do the explanations for its moves.
What's not in question is that during the past few weeks it spiked to levels not seen in over a decade and drove the latest leg of the bond selloff that's sent US Treasury yields to a 24-year high. And that, in turn, is fanning fears of a potential shift that will heap pressure on an already battered market and keep borrowing costs elevated across the economy.
That term premium is essentially protection against unpredictable turns, ranging from geopolitical shocks to government fiscal crises, that could hit the market before long-term bonds come due.
It's distinct from the current outlook for inflation and the direction of monetary policy, both of which are also reflected in yields. Because the premium isn't directly observable and must be inferred, Neel Kashkari, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, once likened it to dark matter, the invisible substance physicists say explains some cosmic mysteries.
"There's multiple ways to calculate it, but they're all going higher," said Frank Rybinski, head of macro strategy at Aegon Asset Management. "And what that tells me is that this move has staying power."
What Bloomberg's Strategists Say...
"The sharp repricing of term premium embedded in Treasuries — with 10-year term premium breaking out to a 12-year high — suggests investors are demanding greater compensation for holding duration amid mounting fiscal and geopolitical uncertainty."
— Frank Monkam, Macro Markets Strategist
There was no clear-cut catalyst. Barclays researchers led by Demi Hu said macroeconomic uncertainty, breakdowns in the usual correlations between stock and bond moves, the rising supply of debt and worries about fiscal policy are all things that figure into the term premium and could be playing a role.
Neil Shearing, the group chief economist at Capital Economics, said the recent move could reflect technical factors, like portfolio adjustments at the end of last month, or the side effects of mounting concern in Europe about France's debt load. Stephen Douglass, chief economist at NISA Investment Advisors, pointed to some indications of stress in credit markets, as well as broader doubts among investors over the benefits of holding fixed-income assets when inflationary shocks are becoming more frequent.
"It's not a simple story," said Douglass, who warned against reading too much into short-term moves. "But I would say that I think we are in a rising term-premium environment."
That's a worry for bond bulls. A structurally higher term premium could keep long-term interest rates elevated, preventing the market from rebounding from its slump.
The metric came down steadily in the 1990s, when increasing globalization was exerting a deflationary force, and fell further still during the 2010s as central banks' quantitative-easing programs distorted global bond markets by flooding them with cash. It dropped as low as negative 1.7% in March 2020, when investors were rushing for the safety of bonds, before rising consistently into positive territory after late 2024, according to a model created by economists working for the New York Fed.
It had remained relatively steady during most of the selloff that started after the US launched its war against Iran in late February.
Then, in mid-September, it started surging. The New York Fed model shows it climbed around 40 basis points to about 0.98%, the highest since 2014 and more than enough to account for the nearly 30 basis-point rise in 10-year Treasury yields over that time. Bloomberg Economics' estimate shows a similar increase. Another, which incorporates economists' forecasts for Fed policy into the calculation, has climbed to 1.08%, the most since 2010.
That break higher came as other drivers of prices were little changed. Inflation expectations have been stable. The Fed's unanimous decision to raise rates last month quelled some concerns about its commitment to reining in consumer prices. And oil, while elevated at over $100 a barrel, has been holding in a narrow range.
A sustained term-premium increase would add to the pressure on the market from elevated inflation, robust economic growth, plus a flood of borrowing from companies investing in artificial intelligence and from deficit-running governments around the globe. Fed Bank of Dallas President Lorie Logan last week said a rising term premium, by pushing up borrowing costs, may slow the economy and reduce the need for the central bank to hike rates.
"The bond market is no longer waiting for the Fed to tighten financial conditions," said Florian Ielpo, head of macro at Lombard Odier Investment Managers. "High term premia, inflation uncertainty and government borrowing needs can keep longer-dated yields restrictive even when the expected path of short rates becomes less aggressive."
One reason behind the latest moves may be spillover effects from the disorderly selloff in French bonds. Some also point to hedging activity by holders of mortgage-backed securities that can temporarily exaggerate market moves.
Yet behind it may be lurking longer-term risks that have been building up in the global economy. One is that shocks to the supply of energy and other commodities — like those that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the US war on Iran — may become more frequent as geopolitical divisions widen.
Then there's the federal government's $2 trillion budget deficit — the equivalent of about 6% of the nation's gross domestic product, an historically high level of stimulus at a time of low unemployment and solid economic growth. While the Trump administration has repeatedly vowed to rein in spending, there's little expectation that will happen anytime soon.
"The macro picture is full of risk which should translate into a healthy term premium," said Mark Malek, the chief investment officer at Siebert Financial. "Any time we have a headline flair up, investors are reminded of that risk."
--With assistance from Christopher Anstey.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
articles.content_orig:
The ⁠ICC’s deputy prosecutor condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal’s work
Navi Pillay has begun giving a press conference after the declaration that she has won this year’s Nobel Peace prize. She began by saying she dedicates the award to “survivors of international crimes”.
She called on people to stand together in the defence of rule of law.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today .
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza ( 11:02 , 11:04 , 11:06 , 11:11 ).
In her first reaction, Pillay specifically paid tribute to all people defending human rights everywhere, as she joked to her associates that “if you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump” ( 11:53 , 12:02 ).
Her win was widely celebrated by senior judges and human right campaigners, who offered their congratulations ( 11:33 , 12:06 , 12:17 , 12:21 , 13:22 , 15:25 ), including the president of the international court of justice, of which she is a former judge ( 12:58 ).
But Israel reacted angrily to the award, saying that “it’s the grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice” ( 13:52 ).
US president Donald Trump also reposted a critical comment saying the Nobel committee “shamed itself beyond repair and demeaned” the prize ( 16:06 ).
Just hours after the announcement, which was explicitly meant as the Nobel Committee’s backing for the international court of justice, the US has imposed sanctions on the court ( 16:20 ).

When the British government announced sweeping sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements and condemned “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank by state-backed “settler terrorists”, some EU diplomats hoped this dramatic shift in UK government policy towards Israel would have a galvanising effect on the rest of Europe. So far, it has not.
Although France and Canada joined the UK in pledging to ban goods from illegal settlements and impose sanctions on “those who facilitate them or profit from them”, there has not yet been a wider ripple effect.
A meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers on Monday is likely to showcase the bloc’s stasis in policy towards Israel – a stalemate that is at odds with rising public criticism in Europe of Israel’s government.
A survey of 10 European countries, including Spain, France and Sweden, found large majorities of people had a negative opinion of Israel. Views had become more negative compared with the previous year, according to the Pew Research Center, mostly after the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which unleashed a new crisis in the Middle East and a global economic shock. In Poland, negative views jumped eight points to 70% of respondents, in Italy they increased by nine points to 75% and in Germany they also rose by nine points to 73%.
Israel is facing ever deeper isolation in the theatre of public opinion. Five countries chose to boycott the Eurovision song contest this year over Israel’s participation, after organisers declined to exclude it over its conduct in the Gaza war and rising violence in the West Bank. Organisers have now decided that broadcasters will no longer be eligible to host the song contest if their state is involved in an armed conflict or sensitive geopolitical situation.
More than 74,000 people, including at least 21,200 children, have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its war in retaliation for the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, in which the terrorist group killed 1,209 people – including 36 children – and took 251 hostages, inflicting a nationwide trauma .
Gaza remains a humanitarian catastrophe , with people facing acute shortages of water, nutritious food and medical equipment and medicines, while contending with disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the threat of death or injury. Israel’s airstrikes continue: the death toll includes 1,400 Palestinians killed since a ceasefire was declared a year ago.
The EU talks on the Middle East will focus on the conflicts in Iran and Yemen, but ministers will also discuss the situation in Gaza and the West Bank in the context of elections in Israel on 27 October and the first legislative elections in Palestine in 20 years, which are expected by late November.
The discussion is expected to expose familiar fault lines in the 27-member EU. One group of countries are vocal supporters of the Palestinian cause: Spain and Ireland were the first to call for a review of whether Israel’s conduct in the Gaza war was in breach of the human rights requirements of its association agreement with the EU, which covers the €68bn (£58bn) trade relationship, cooperation in research, environment and energy.
A second group consistently opposes targeting Israel’s government: Germany and Austria are close allies for historical reasons, while Czechia and Italy are ideologically aligned with Benjamin Netanyahu’s administration.
Among a third, larger group of countries in the middle are several, such as France and the Netherlands, that are increasingly critical of the Netanyahu government’s conduct in Gaza and its plans to build the vast E1 settlement, which threatens to critically damage the two-state solution.
Czechs go to the polls on Friday at the start of two days of voting to fill one-third of the seats in Parliament’s upper house, the Senate, and elect local representatives, AP reported.
The elections are the first test for populist billionaire Andrej Babiš since he returned to power after a decisive victory in parliamentary elections in October 2025.
His centrist ANO (YES) movement hopes to make gains in the 81-seat Senate, which is controlled by pro-western opposition parties. Twenty-seven Senate seats are up for grabs in the two-round election, with runoffs scheduled for next week. First-round results are expected on Saturday.
Babiš has formed a governing coalition with two small political groups whose agenda includes reducing support for Ukraine and rejecting some key European Union policies.
Unlike the government, the opposition and president Petr Pavel remain firm supporters of Ukraine following Russia’s invasion.
But Pavel – an avid biker – attracted a lot of attention in the build up to the vote as it emerged that he would miss the vote due to a long-planned motorcycle trip in Morocco. After days of relentless pressure, he eventually cut the holiday short and reported to vote, acknowledging his original “error” in scheduling.
“Some mistakes can be corrected relatively easily, others with more difficulty, and some cannot be corrected at all.
Fortunately, a mistake in planning can be remedied by changing the plan. Admitting a mistake is not easy, but if a politician values people’s trust, he must prove it.
I know what responsibility is and that any trust is hard to earn, but terribly easy and quick to lose. You pay for mistakes, and I have learned from this one of my own.”
The European Union is granting temporary trade preferences to Armenia following trade restrictions recently imposed by Russia.
In a move which shows how flexible the EU can be, it said the temporary trade preferences “will help alleviate the difficult situation faced by Armenian producers and exporters and support the resilience of Armenia’s economy by facilitating access to the EU market.
The measures, which will enter into force tomorrow for a period of two years, temporarily allow 80% of Armenian exports to the EU, including almost all exports of fresh fruit, vegetables and flowers affected by the Russian measures, as well as over 91% of exports of beverages and spirits.
Armenia is not an accession state, but has been singled out for support as part of the EU a broader solidarity support package

articles.title_orig: A Taste of the World, Here at Home in Fayetteville
articles.title_zh: A Taste of the World, Here at Home in Fayetteville
articles.content_orig:
This story first appeared in CityView magazine’s October 2026 edition.
From Afghan kabobs and West African fare to Japanese ramen, Filipino favorites, and Southern barbecue, Fayetteville’s dining scene offers a rich history of reflecting the many cultures that have long called the city home.
It’s a cultural diversity that is beautifully on display in the breadth of restaurants, cafes, food trucks, and family kitchens scattered throughout Cumberland County.
That diversity has helped create a notable food scene: Today, more than 600 restaurants are listed across the Fayetteville area. It has largely eschewed trendy, upscale spots in favor of affordable, hyper-authentic strip mall joints and small family-owned eateries that were designed to give back to homesick soldiers, military spouses, and veterans who have lived, and eaten, all over the world.
Food is often the first entry point into connection, crossing divides that otherwise might seem insurmountable. With food, we get family recipes, intimate traditions, surprising commonalities and, above all, a true generosity of spirit. Cooking and eating is service in its most human form, a labor-infused gift from the chef to those who are hungry.
On any given day in the city, your meal could be Afghan kabobs and rice as easily as it could be Japanese ramen, Vietnamese pho, or Thai curry. There is Filipino lumpia, West African fufu and stews, Puerto Rican specialties, rich Mediterranean and Middle Eastern dishes, Indian curries, and tandoori cooking. In areas like Cliffdale Square, you can find a German bakery, an Indian restaurant, a Puerto Rican diner, and a Japanese hibachi spot sharing the same parking lot.
At Germène’s Home Kitchen & Bakery on Robeson Street, which opened just this year, owner and operations manager Eddy Claude shares food rooted in his upbringing.
Born and raised in Haiti, where he owned his first restaurant, Claude spent nearly 21 years in the U.S. Army. His Fayetteville restaurant grew from simple roots: weekend gatherings where Claude cooked traditional food for family and friends.
Eventually, encouragement from those around him helped turn those gatherings into a permanent restaurant, and the name itself is a tribute to Claude’s late grandmother, Germène.
“She was a loving and generous woman who believed that everyone who came to her home should be welcomed and fed, whether or not they had money,” Claude said. “I wanted the restaurant to continue her legacy of feeding people and caring for them. That is also the meaning behind our motto: ‘Cooking with love.’”
Every one of Fayetteville’s international restaurants, from the most modest grab-and-go to the priciest sit-down spot, tells the story of one family’s foodway.
On Person Street, diners can find Taste of West Africa, a Ghana-focused restaurant serving traditional West African soups, fufu, rice dishes, and stews. Mai’s Kitchen brings Thai cooking to the downtown area. There’s delicious Vietnamese food at places like Vietnam Kitchen or Saigon Bistro. Afghan Kabob serves grilled kabobs, rice plates and other Afghan and Middle Eastern fare on Raeford Road, and the much-loved Pharaohs Village serves traditional Egyptian fava bean falafel, shish taouk, and halal platters.
There is rich Indian food, too, along with boldly flavored Caribbean, Puerto Rican, Filipino, Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Mexican, and Italian restaurants. For diners, the city’s food scene is something of a culinary passport.
At Ichi-Kaku Japanese Restaurant, owner and executive chef Yohei Kamiya thinks of his restaurant as a small doorway connecting Japan and Fayetteville—an idea that speaks to the larger role international restaurants can play in a city like this one.
Kamiya grew up in Nagoya, Japan, and worked in Japanese restaurants in New York and North Carolina before opening Ichi-Kaku in 2022.
Kamiya wanted his restaurant to do more than simply reproduce familiar Japanese dishes. He wanted the flavors, aromas, and temperatures of the food to carry some of the emotion and memory associated with his home country.
When Ichi-Kaku opened, Kamiya had his family’s support from the beginning. His sons, Alex and Max, worked alongside him, his daughter Michelle provided moral support, and his wife Tara managed operations. Kamiya ran the kitchen himself seven days a week. After approximately six months, the team began to grow gradually to its current team of 15 people.
Today, the menu includes Ichi-Kaku Signature Ramen, built around a tonkotsu-based pork and chicken broth with dashi made from ingredients including shiitake, kombu, bonito, and mackerel. Chicken katsu curry and crispy Wagyu gyoza are among the other popular dishes.
That same sense of familiarity is at the heart of Kusinera Filipino Cuisine on Legion Road, owned by Esperanza “Nanette” Thomas and her husband, David.
Nanette’s interest in Filipino cooking began with the dishes she grew up eating, and the restaurant grew from her passion for sharing those foods with others. For her, Filipino food is closely tied to family, gathering, sharing, and belonging.
At Kusinera, diners can indulge in a platter filled with steamed rice, pancit, lumpia, fried pork belly, grilled pork belly, and chicken and pork skewers. Shanghai lumpia, pancit and sisig are among the other Filipino favorites on the menu.
The Thomases say Fayetteville has welcomed them, providing a place where they know Filipino families can find familiar flavors and where diners who have never experienced Filipino cooking can discover something new to love.
That dual purpose—dishing up a taste of home and providing a humble introduction to something new—is part of what makes food so communal. Across Fayetteville, diners are afforded the gift of flavors from countries and cultures that perhaps aren’t primarily associated with North Carolinian cuisine.
There is, certainly, barbecue, fried chicken, and sweet tea here. Chefs at eateries like Circa 1800 do thoughtful work around using local farms and seasonal ingredients that pay homage to the area. There are burgers, pizza, brunch, and bakeries. Longtime local institutions exist alongside newer restaurants and food trucks. But here, as much as anywhere in the state, global fare thrives alongside Southern favorites.
And the dining options only continue to grow. Fayetteville’s current landscape gives diners an ever-expanding number of ways to experience their community through food. According to The Fayetteville Observer , last year alone another 50 restaurants joined the city. The scene is a reflection of the people who live here—a melting pot in the truest sense. Each restaurant, from Ohana International to Desde Mi Balcón Restaurant and SimLo’s Island Cafe, lets diners see where each individual restaurateur has come from, what they grew up eating, what they chose to bring with them and what they’ve integrated when they arrived.
Either way, the invitation is essentially the same: Pull up a seat, try something new, bring someone you love with you. There are plenty of tables waiting for us all.

articles.title_orig: World News in Brief: ‘Horrific’ attack Sudan, Israeli incursions in Syria intensify, most women and girls homeless in Gaza
articles.title_zh: World News in Brief: ‘Horrific’ attack Sudan, Israeli incursions in Syria intensify, most women and girls homeless in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
A suspected drone strike has left at least 40 dead in Sudan’s Blue Nile State – near the Ethiopian border - according to initial reports from the ground, according to UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric. Most of the casualties were women and girls.
Fighting in the region has escalated in the last few months as clashes have intensified between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Government.
They are fighting over strategic towns and bases near the Ethiopian border, as part of the broader battle for control of Sudan that has been ongoing since April 2023.
In recent weeks, thousands of civilians have been displaced in the area due to sustained attacks.
Mr. Dujarric condemned the “horrifying reports” stressing that attacks directed towards civilians are prohibited under international humanitarian law.
He called for those responsible for these violations to be held accountable.
Israeli military incursions into southern Syria are intensifying, with some 280 incidents recorded in September alone – the highest monthly figure this year, the UN human rights office ( OHCHR ) said on Friday.
The incidents include reported raids on homes, restrictions on movement, harassment of civilians and arbitrary detention.
Spokesperson Shabia Mantoo said 49 Syrians are believed to remain in Israeli custody, though the figure has not been independently verified.
Former detainees describe detention lasting over a year in some cases, no reasons given and transfers to unknown facilities. They also allege torture and ill-treatment, including beatings, prolonged forced standing and threats to their families.
On Monday, a 22-year-old man from Jaba town in Quneitra governorate was killed by Israeli forces near Al-Hamidiyah.
He was reportedly walking at night and did not know an Israeli military position lay ahead. No warning shots are known to have been fired.
On Wednesday, a farmer with a disability was reportedly shot in the leg during an incursion in northern Quneitra, then detained while bleeding and released an hour and a half later.
High Commissioner Volker Türk called for a “prompt and impartial investigation” into the killing and urged Israel to stop harassing civilians.
In Gaza, nearly 50,000 women and girls have been killed or severely injured since the start of the Hamas-Israel war in October 2023, according to the specialised UN agency UN Women .
This includes more than 38,000 killed and 11,700 left with injuries so severe that they now live with lifelong disabilities.
Today, almost all women and girls have been forced from their homes, and most are now living in tents or amid the ruins of their homes.
Women now lead one in four households in the Strip, often while facing deeper poverty and repeated displacement with increasingly limited resources.
UN Women’s Sofia Calltorp told the story of Nour, one of the women behind this statistic.
Her home was destroyed, and her husband, a nurse, was detained – she has not heard from him since. At times, she says she becomes so lost in thought that she is unable to respond even to her children.
At the same time, because of funding cuts, nearly two thirds of the organizations contacted by the agency in Gaza and the occupied West Bank said they have been forced to put women and girls on waiting lists or turn them away altogether.
Every organization surveyed also reported an increase in gender-based violence, poverty and mental health distress since 2025. And all but one had seen an increase in child marriage.

articles.title_orig: Google officially teases Fitbit Edge tracker, confirms October 12 launch
articles.title_zh: Google officially teases Fitbit Edge tracker, confirms October 12 launch
articles.content_orig:
Google has dropped an official teaser for its Fitbit Edge tracker and confirmed an October 12 launch, just a few days away.
In a brief post on social media ( Twitter/X , Instagram ) Google simply says:
Get an Edge on your health. 10.12.2026.
It’s simple and to the point, and says a lot while not saying much at all. The teaser confirms the “Edge” branding of the new tracker, which is said to follow the Air in Fitbit hardware lineup. The Fitbit Edge is then confirmed to launch on October 12, this coming Monday.
Google’s teaser image just barely hints at the display we’ve seen in leaks, while also confirming that the company’s “Canyon” color scheme will continue through from the Pixel Watch 5. It’s also obvious that the Edge has a metal chassis.
Other leaks have detailed 7-day battery life, Gemini integration, iPhone support, and more for the upcoming Fitbit Edge. Pricing is expected to be around $180 — not too far above the screen-less Fitbit Air, but well below the Pixel Watch 5’s $400 entry price.

articles.title_orig: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
articles.title_zh: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
articles.content_orig:
Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice
US politics – live updates
If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.
Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International .
In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.
In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.
Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.
Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.
Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.
Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.
In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook .
The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.
In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.
Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December . Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.
Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.
In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran , its highest number of executions in decades.
Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.
“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

articles.title_orig: Northern Lights could be visible in Capital Region this weekend
articles.title_zh: Northern Lights could be visible in Capital Region this weekend
articles.content_orig:
The ejection is associated with a moderate solar flare.
It's been a busy week for the sun, and aurora watchers in some northern and upper Midwest states looking for a glimpse of the famed colorful sky could benefit from enhanced solar activity Thursday night into Friday morning, Oct. 9.
On Tuesday, a coronal mass ejection (CME), a massive burst of charged particles embedded in a magnetic field, departed the sun bound for Earth.
The ejection is associated with a moderate solar flare.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) has issued a moderate Geomagnetic Storm Watch beginning Thursday evening into Friday, as a result of the CME.
According to NOAA , a geomagnetic storm is "a major disturbance of Earth's magnetosphere that occurs when there is a very efficient exchange of energy from the solar wind into the space environment surrounding Earth."
While the agency says much of the activity will be minor, there could be periods of moderate storm activity. The UK Met Office says there's even a slight chance of strong G3 levels.
The SWPC says the solar activity could create minor impacts to our technological infrastructure, but it's "mainly manageable."
On the bright side, the aurora borealis, which appears in the night sky when electrically charged particles from the sun hit Earth's atmosphere, could be visible in areas that don't normally experience it.
"Aurora may be seen as low as New York to Wisconsin to Washington state," SWPC said in its alert.
Another CME linked to a smaller solar flare is also headed toward Earth but is only expected to deliver a "glancing blow" over the weekend, according to the UK Met Office.
All this solar weather will keep conditions unsettled to active over the next few days. But whether you'll be able to see the auroras depends on exactly when the CME arrives, the cloud cover and the magnetic orientation of the CME's magnetic field.
When geomagnetic activity becomes stronger, the aurora can sometimes be seen farther south than usual.

articles.title_orig: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
articles.title_zh: Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?
articles.content_orig:
Prices for gasoline and diesel have more than doubled since the US-Israel conflict with Iran began in February, affecting transport businesses, farmers and anyone who drives a vehicle in America.
Ahead of the critical midterm elections, there have been growing calls for more to be done to reduce the price of fuel, and US President Donald Trump has made several comments and announcements aimed at getting costs down.
With just a few weeks to go before Americans head to the polls, Trump on Friday announced a deal with President Vladimir Putin for Russian diesel to be released immediately to the US and global markets.
He said this included the immediate supply of over 300,000 tonnes, 500,000 tonnes in November and a further million tonnes "immediately thereafter".
He said this would mean diesel prices in the US and across the world "will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!".
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
He added that a further 3m tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period" after, dependent on the condition of its refineries.
Trump's announcement of a waiver on the use of red dye diesel at a campaign stop this week underscored the importance of gas prices in a midterm election dominated by affordability issues.
The election comes as there is widespread public concern over the rising costs of fuel, food and other goods. Voters have tied the issue to Trump and his party, weighing down Republicans running in November.
Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, which has contributed to high diesel and gas prices in the US.
Global oil supplies have been restricted since the conflict in the Middle East effectively halted the usual flow of oil and refined products through the Strait of Hormuz for months.
While the flow of crude oil is nearly back to pre-war levels the price remains above $100 a barrel, and sustained high oil prices have had a knock-on effect for diesel and gasoline.
David Ruisard, pricing manager for commodities intelligence firm Argus says the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine has also impacted oil supplies, contributing to higher fuel prices.
"Our estimates are that your price increase from about $3 a gallon up to $6 a gallon [for diesel] is 60% connected to the Strait of Hormuz, 40% connected to the Russia-Ukraine conflict," he says.
Those higher energy prices are responsible for most of the uptick in inflation this year, Oxford Economics chief US economist Michael Pearce says, which is pushing up interest rates.
"The combined impact of higher rates and higher energy prices is squeezing household budgets and adding to firms' costs," he says.
While prices remain high, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for fuel price tracking website GasBuddy said there have been modest declines recently for both gasoline and diesel.
"A lot of that is likely due to some of the manoeuvres that we've seen the Trump administration employ over the last couple of weeks," he said.
Friday's diesel announcement is the latest in a series of policies and ideas announced by Trump.
The president announced this week that he would allow so-called red dye diesel - fuel which is used off-road and does not face federal taxes - to be used on US highways without facing federal levies.
Ruisard said the only difference in the diesel used by truck drivers and everyday consumers and the tax-free red dye diesel is the dye itself.
"The problem with that red dye is, it's extremely hard to clean it out of your tank," he explained.
The problem that creates is what happens to trucking companies that use the dyed diesel once the temporary tax relief ends, he said.
"The fines are pretty high for having that in your fuel tank because its considered tax evasion."
The other issue with expanding the use of red dye diesel, according to Ruisard, is that people and businesses - including rail operators - usually set aside a particular amount of the product.
"If suddenly people go out and they start consuming that diesel, that depletes their available supply as well," he said.
But another move from Trump has been more successful, according to analysts.
Last week, the G7 countries announced they would release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to ease supply concerns , following pressure from Trump to do so.
De Haan says the announcement itself – regardless of how much has been released so far – "has worked to push prices down to some degree".
Economist Pearce agreed but warned the release is only a temporary solution.
"As long as energy exports from the Gulf remain disrupted, stocks will need to be drained further to supply the market," he said. "And the need to refill those stocks will mean energy prices remain elevated for a period, even when disruption in the Middle East clears."
Earlier this week, Trump said he was "thinking about" suspending federal tax on gasoline.
De Haan said the president has also been imploring states to cut state taxes on gasoline and several have done so, including Ohio and Georgia.
State taxes form a "moderate portion" of what consumers pay at the pump, and those reductions have helped reduce prices and national averages, he said.
However, suspending or reducing the federal levy on gasoline would require the cooperation of Congress.
"That may be difficult to obtain ahead of the midterm elections," said De Haan.
It is also a costly measure.
De Haan estimated that in Indiana, which cut its tax on gasoline in May, it has cost the state government $1bn (£760m) in lost revenue.
Trump has also previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.
While that would provide partial relief in the Gulf and Midwest, according to Pearce, he adds it would be of "little benefit" to the Northeast and West Coast.
"The policy risks backfiring because it would result in stockpiling of diesel, and as that storage runs out, refineries would need to cut back on production," he said.
"That would raise prices of other energy products, including gasoline."
De Haan believes the president has "basically pulled all of the small levers that a president can pull, and we're still seeing prices very elevated".
"The only way out of this to reduce gas prices in a meaningful way is solve one or both of the geopolitical tensions that are causing high prices," he said.
That means reaching a deal with Iran and helping facilitate an agreement between Ukraine and Russia - which, Pearce said, are issues that cannot be directly controlled by the White House.
Even if those conflicts are resolved, Ruisard said that due to damage to facilities in the Middle East caused by military strikes it would still take production four to six months to return to normal.
"The message to consumers and industry is that regardless of what happens and whether the president is able to successfully negotiate that kind of a deal," he said.
"High prices are here to stay for a little while at least."
Additional reporting from Daniel Bush
